title: SSH Brute Force Against RHEL Host
description: Detects a high volume of failed SSH password authentication attempts against a single RHEL host from one source, consistent with brute-force password guessing. Attackers use this against internet-facing or improperly segmented SSH endpoints; legitimate users rarely fail more than 2-3 times before giving up or requesting a reset.

data_sources.name: sshd (secure log)
data_sources.description: sshd logs every authentication attempt with outcome, method, source IP, and username.

detection_logic: Counts distinct failed-password events per source IP against a host within a rolling window; a source producing many failures against few or many usernames in a short window is characteristic of automated guessing rather than human error.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure "Failed password" OR "authentication failure"
| rex field=_raw "Failed password for (invalid user )?(?<user>\S+) from (?<src_ip>\S+)"
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count as failures dc(user) as distinct_users values(user) as users by _time, host, src_ip
| where failures >= 10
tuning_guidance: Vulnerability scanners, misconfigured monitoring agents, and expired automation credentials retrying on a schedule are the main false-positive sources. Allowlist known scanner/jump-host IPs and any automation account whose retry behavior is understood.
investigation_steps: Identify src_ip and whether it is a known jump host, VPN egress, or scanner.
Check whether any of the attempted usernames subsequently succeeded (see RHEL-002).
Check for the same src_ip against other RHEL hosts in the fleet (lateral brute-force sweep).
response_guidance: Block or rate-limit the source at the firewall/fail2ban layer, verify no attempted username authenticated successfully, and rotate credentials for any account that did.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Successful SSH Login Following Repeated Failures
description: Detects a successful SSH authentication for a user/source pair that recently produced multiple failed attempts - the classic signature of a brute-force or password-spray attempt that ultimately succeeded. This is one of the highest-confidence credential-compromise indicators available from authentication logs alone.

data_sources.name: sshd (secure log)
data_sources.description: Correlates Failed password and Accepted password/publickey events for the same user/src_ip.

detection_logic: A join/subsearch pattern matches an Accepted event to a preceding burst of Failed events for the same user and source within a short window; legitimate interactive logins essentially never follow 5+ failures from the same source.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure "Accepted password" OR "Accepted publickey"
| rex field=_raw "Accepted \S+ for (?<user>\S+) from (?<src_ip>\S+)"
| rename _time as success_time
| join type=inner user src_ip
    [ search index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure "Failed password"
      | rex field=_raw "Failed password for (invalid user )?(?<user>\S+) from (?<src_ip>\S+)"
      | bin _time span=15m
      | stats count as prior_failures by _time, host, user, src_ip
      | where prior_failures >= 5 ]
| table success_time, host, user, src_ip, prior_failures
tuning_guidance: Users who mistype passwords a handful of times before succeeding, or key-based clients that also attempt (and fail) password auth first due to client misconfiguration, can trigger this at low volume. Tune the failure threshold up for hosts with known-flaky clients.
investigation_steps: Confirm with the account owner whether the login was expected.
Review commands executed in the resulting session (auditd EXECVE, shell history).
Check for lateral movement or privilege escalation immediately following the login.
response_guidance: Treat as a likely compromised credential: disable/rotate the account, terminate the session, and review all activity performed under it since the successful login.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Direct Root SSH Login
description: Detects a successful SSH session authenticated directly as root, rather than an unprivileged user escalating via sudo/su. Direct root login is disabled by best practice (PermitRootLogin no) precisely because it removes per-user accountability; its use - successful or attempted - is a strong signal of either misconfiguration or an attacker who already has the root credential/key.

data_sources.name: sshd (secure log)
data_sources.description: Accepted password/publickey events with user=root.

detection_logic: Filters accepted SSH authentication events to user=root; in a hardened environment this should almost never fire outside a documented break-glass procedure.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure "Accepted" "for root from"
| rex field=_raw "Accepted (?<method>\S+) for root from (?<src_ip>\S+)"
| table _time, host, src_ip, method
tuning_guidance: Break-glass/emergency access procedures and some backup/imaging appliances legitimately use root SSH; maintain an allowlist of source IPs and require a change ticket for any use outside it.
investigation_steps: Confirm src_ip against the break-glass allowlist and any open change ticket.
Review sshd_config for PermitRootLogin to confirm it should be disabled.
Review commands executed as root in the session.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, disable PermitRootLogin, rotate the root credential/authorized_keys, and investigate the source for compromise.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: SSH Password Authentication Where Key-Only Is Expected
description: Detects successful password-based SSH authentication on hosts/users that normally authenticate exclusively via public key. A sudden appearance of password auth can indicate an attacker who obtained a password but not a key, or that PasswordAuthentication was re-enabled to create an easier access path (see RHEL-018).

data_sources.name: sshd (secure log)
data_sources.description: Accepted password vs. Accepted publickey events.

detection_logic: Builds a per-user/per-host baseline of authentication method over a trailing period and flags a password-method event for a user/host pair whose baseline is 100% publickey.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure "Accepted"
| rex field=_raw "Accepted (?<method>\S+) for (?<user>\S+) from"
| eval is_password=if(method="password",1,0)
| stats count(eval(method="password")) as pw_count, count(eval(method="publickey")) as key_count by host, user
| where key_count > 0 AND pw_count > 0
tuning_guidance: Password auth used once during initial provisioning before a key is deployed, or by a break-glass account, is expected; suppress for the provisioning window and known break-glass accounts.
investigation_steps: Check whether sshd_config for the host was recently changed (RHEL-018).
Confirm with the user whether they used a password intentionally.
Review the source IP against the user's normal baseline.
response_guidance: If unexpected, treat the account's password as compromised, rotate it, and confirm PasswordAuthentication is disabled again if it should be.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: SSH Authentication From Unusual Source IP
description: Detects a successful SSH login from a source IP never previously observed for that user/host pair. A first-seen source for an established administrator account is a common early indicator of credential theft or use from an attacker-controlled pivot host.

data_sources.name: sshd (secure log)
data_sources.description: Source IP and user of accepted SSH sessions.

detection_logic: Baseline implementation: maintain a lookup of (user, src_ip) pairs seen in a trailing 90-day window; flag any accepted login whose (user, src_ip) is not in the lookup. Simple implementation: flag logins from IP ranges outside your documented administrative CIDR blocks.
spl:
`comment("Simple implementation")`
index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure "Accepted" NOT [ | inputlookup admin_cidr_allowlist.csv | fields src_ip ]
| rex field=_raw "Accepted \S+ for (?<user>\S+) from (?<src_ip>\S+)"
| table _time, host, user, src_ip

`comment("Baseline-oriented implementation")`
| tstats count where index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure by user, src_ip
| lookup ssh_user_src_baseline.csv user, src_ip OUTPUT is_known
| where isnull(is_known)
tuning_guidance: New employees, IP changes from ISPs/mobile carriers, VPN egress rotation, and DR failover all produce legitimate first-seen sources; keep the baseline lookup refreshed and expect a higher volume immediately after any network change.
investigation_steps: Geolocate/ASN-check the new source IP.
Confirm with the user whether they are traveling, on a new connection, or using a new jump host.
Check for subsequent privileged activity from the session.
response_guidance: If unconfirmed, treat as investigate-first rather than block-first to avoid disrupting legitimate access changes; escalate to account lockout only if corroborated by other signals.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: PAM Authentication Failure Burst
description: Detects a burst of PAM authentication failures across any service (login, su, sudo, sshd, gdm) for a single user or source, which can indicate brute-forcing at the PAM layer rather than SSH specifically (e.g. against console login or a locally-exposed service using PAM).

data_sources.name: PAM (syslog/secure log)
data_sources.description: pam_unix and related PAM modules log authentication failure with the service name and user.

detection_logic: Counts PAM authentication-failure log lines per user across all PAM-consuming services in a rolling window.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure "pam_unix" "authentication failure"
| rex field=_raw "\((?<service>\S+)\).*user=(?<user>\S+)"
| bin _time span=10m
| stats count as failures values(service) as services by _time, host, user
| where failures >= 8
tuning_guidance: Shared kiosk/console accounts and misconfigured automation retrying a stale password are common sources; exclude known shared-console hostnames from alerting or route them to a lower-severity queue.
investigation_steps: Identify which PAM service(s) are involved.
Check for a subsequent successful authentication for the same user.
Correlate with physical/console access logs if the service is login/gdm.
response_guidance: Lock the account if failures continue past a reasonable threshold and investigate the source (console session, service caller).
author: Threat Detection Library

title: PAM Configuration File Modified
description: Detects modification of files under /etc/pam.d/ or /etc/pam.conf. PAM configuration controls how every authentication decision on the host is made; attackers modify it to weaken authentication requirements (e.g. removing pam_faillock, adding a permissive module) or to install a credential-harvesting/backdoor PAM module that grants access with any password.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: File-write watch on /etc/pam.d/ and /etc/pam.conf via auditd.

detection_logic: auditd watch rule on the PAM config directory generates a PATH/SYSCALL event pair for every write; the search surfaces the writing process, its real user (auid, which survives sudo/su), and the modified path.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=PATH (path="/etc/pam.d/*" OR path="/etc/pam.conf")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| rex field=_raw "exe=\"(?<exe>[^\"]+)\""
| table _time, host, auid, exe, path, key
tuning_guidance: Configuration management (Ansible/Satellite/RPM package updates to pam packages) legitimately modifies these files; correlate against AAP job execution (RH-X-003) or a package-manager transaction (RPM install/update) before treating as suspicious.
investigation_steps: Diff the modified file against the last known-good version.
Identify auid and whether it corresponds to a human, an AAP job, or a package update.
Check for a new/unfamiliar module reference (pam_*.so) added to the stack.
response_guidance: Restore from known-good configuration management state immediately; treat the host as compromised if the change cannot be attributed to authorized configuration management.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1556.003: Pluggable Authentication Modules

author: Threat Detection Library

title: su Failures Against Privileged Accounts
description: Detects repeated failed `su` attempts, particularly targeting root or other privileged accounts, indicating an attacker with a foothold is trying to guess the target account's password to escalate locally.

data_sources.name: PAM/su (secure log)
data_sources.description: su logs authentication result with target user.

detection_logic: Counts failed su authentication attempts by the invoking user and target account in a rolling window.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure "su:" "FAILED su for"
| rex field=_raw "FAILED su for (?<target_user>\S+) by (?<user>\S+)"
| bin _time span=10m
| stats count as failures by _time, host, user, target_user
| where failures >= 5
tuning_guidance: Developers/admins who forget the root password on a rarely-used box will trigger a handful of failures; the threshold and repeated-across-hosts pattern separate this from an attacker's escalation attempt.
investigation_steps: Identify the invoking user and whether they hold legitimate access to the target account.
Check for a subsequent successful su or sudo escalation.
Review the invoking user's session for how they obtained their foothold.
response_guidance: Investigate the invoking account for compromise; if the target account password is weak/shared, rotate it.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1548.003: Sudo and Sudo Caching

author: Threat Detection Library

title: sudo Authentication Failures
description: Detects repeated sudo password failures for a user, which can indicate an attacker who has a foothold under a low-privilege account and is guessing that account's own password to use permitted sudo rules, or probing which commands are allowed.

data_sources.name: sudo (secure log)
data_sources.description: sudo logs authentication failures with the invoking user and attempted command.

detection_logic: Counts sudo authentication-failure log lines per user in a rolling window; a legitimate user typically fails 0-2 times due to typos.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure "sudo:" "authentication failure"
| rex field=_raw "sudo:\s+(?<user>\S+)\s+:"
| bin _time span=10m
| stats count as failures by _time, host, user
| where failures >= 5
tuning_guidance: Users who forget they were logged out of a cached sudo session, or scripts run interactively without an expected TTY, can produce a few failures; tune per-host if a particular team habitually mistypes.
investigation_steps: Check whether the failures were followed by a success (RHEL-010).
Review sudoers rules available to the user for scope of potential access.
Confirm the session's origin (SSH source, prior authentication).
response_guidance: No action needed for isolated low-volume failures; escalate per the fleet correlation in RH-X-002 if the same pattern appears across multiple hosts.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1548.003: Sudo and Sudo Caching

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Unusual sudo Command Execution
description: Detects a sudo invocation running a command the user has not previously run via sudo, especially one granting broad capability (shell, package manager, editor with shell-out, systemctl). A first-seen sudo command for a user is a common signal of an attacker who has gained the account's credential and is exploring what its sudo rule permits.

data_sources.name: sudo (secure log)
data_sources.description: Successful sudo COMMAND= log lines.

detection_logic: Baseline implementation compares each successful sudo COMMAND against a per-user 90-day history; simple implementation flags known shell-escape-capable commands (vi, vim, less, awk, python, perl, find) run via sudo, which are the classic GTFOBins privilege-escalation-to-full-shell pattern.
spl:
`comment("Simple implementation - shell-escape-capable binaries via sudo")`
index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure "sudo:" "COMMAND="
| rex field=_raw "sudo:\s+(?<user>\S+).*COMMAND=(?<command>.+)"
| where match(command, "(?i)(/bin/(ba)?sh|vi(m)?\s|less\s|more\s|awk\s|find\s.*-exec|python[23]?\s|perl\s)")
| table _time, host, user, command

`comment("Baseline-oriented implementation")`
| stats count by user, command
| lookup sudo_user_command_baseline.csv user, command OUTPUT is_known
| where isnull(is_known)
tuning_guidance: Admins legitimately use vi/less/awk via sudo for routine file edits; this is high-value primarily for accounts whose sudoers rule was intended to be narrowly scoped (e.g. `sudo systemctl restart myapp`) and is instead being used to reach a shell.
investigation_steps: Compare the command against the account's documented sudoers rule intent.
Check whether an interactive shell resulted (auid changes to root in subsequent commands).
Review the account's recent authentication history for compromise indicators.
response_guidance: If the command exceeds the account's intended scope, narrow the sudoers rule immediately and investigate the account for compromise.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1548.003: Sudo and Sudo Caching

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Console (Physical/DCUI) Login
description: Detects an interactive login at the local console (tty1-6) rather than over the network. On servers, physical/console access should be rare and tied to a documented data-center visit; unexpected console logins can indicate physical access compromise or use of an out-of-band management interface (iLO/iDRAC virtual console).

data_sources.name: PAM/login (secure log)
data_sources.description: login records tty and user for console sessions.

detection_logic: Filters accepted login events where the tty matches a physical console device rather than a pty (network session).
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure "session opened for user" NOT pts
| rex field=_raw "session opened for user (?<user>\S+)"
| table _time, host, user
tuning_guidance: Data-center technicians performing maintenance, or IPMI/iLO virtual-console access for troubleshooting a hung host, are the expected sources; correlate with change tickets for physical maintenance windows.
investigation_steps: Confirm against a physical access log or data-center visitor log.
Check whether the out-of-band management interface (iLO/iDRAC) shows a session.
Review activity performed during the console session.
response_guidance: Escalate to physical security if no maintenance record exists.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Interactive Login by a Service Account
description: Detects an interactive SSH/console login using an account that is provisioned as a service account (non-interactive shell, no expected human user) - e.g. postgres, apache, nagios, ansible, satellite-service accounts. Attackers who compromise a service credential (often over-privileged and rarely monitored) frequently use it for interactive access since it draws less attention than a human admin account.

data_sources.name: sshd/PAM (secure log)
data_sources.description: Accepted login events matched against a maintained list of service-account usernames.

detection_logic: Joins accepted authentication events against a lookup of known service-account names; any match is anomalous by definition since these accounts should never authenticate interactively.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure "Accepted"
| rex field=_raw "Accepted \S+ for (?<user>\S+) from (?<src_ip>\S+)"
| lookup service_account_list.csv user OUTPUT is_service_account
| where is_service_account=1
| table _time, host, user, src_ip
tuning_guidance: Keep the service-account lookup current as accounts are provisioned/decommissioned; a small number of service accounts are legitimately used for scripted SSH (e.g. an Ansible push user) - exclude those explicitly known cases with source-IP allowlisting rather than removing them from the list entirely.
investigation_steps: Confirm the account's shell is set to nologin/false in /etc/passwd - if so this should be impossible and indicates tampering.
Identify src_ip and compare to any known automation host.
Review commands executed in the session.
response_guidance: Rotate the service account's credential/key immediately and audit all activity performed under it.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Dormant Account Reactivated
description: Detects a successful authentication for an account with no login activity in the preceding 90+ days. Dormant accounts (former employees, decommissioned service accounts, break-glass accounts) are a favored persistence target because their sudden use is unlikely to be noticed by anyone watching for 'normal' account behavior.

data_sources.name: sshd/PAM (secure log)
data_sources.description: Historical login timestamps per account.

detection_logic: Compares the current login's user against a maintained last-seen-login lookup; flags accounts whose prior login is null or older than the dormancy threshold.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_secure "Accepted"
| rex field=_raw "Accepted \S+ for (?<user>\S+) from"
| lookup account_last_login.csv user OUTPUT last_login_time
| eval days_dormant=round((now()-last_login_time)/86400,1)
| where isnull(last_login_time) OR days_dormant > 90
| table _time, host, user, days_dormant
tuning_guidance: Quarterly/annual maintenance accounts and disaster-recovery break-glass credentials are expected to be dormant most of the time; maintain an exception list with documented use cadence.
investigation_steps: Confirm the account should still exist (check HR/offboarding records for human accounts).
Review what the account did once authenticated.
Check whether the account's password/key was recently changed (unexpectedly).
response_guidance: Disable the account pending confirmation of legitimate use; if unauthorized, treat as a confirmed persistence mechanism and investigate how the credential was obtained.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: New UID 0 Account Created
description: Detects creation of a local account with UID 0 (root-equivalent) other than the canonical root account itself. This is one of the most direct persistence mechanisms available on Linux: any account with UID 0 has full root privileges regardless of its name, and a duplicate-UID-0 account is easy to overlook in a casual review of /etc/passwd.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: Watch on /etc/passwd captures the write; useradd/usermod invocation captured via EXECVE.

detection_logic: Watches for writes to /etc/passwd and, where EXECVE telemetry is available, for useradd/usermod invocations with -o -u 0 (the -o flag is required to permit a duplicate UID).
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "a0=\"(?<argv0>[^\"]+)\""
| where match(argv0, "(?i)(useradd|usermod)")
| rex field=_raw "a\d=\"(?<arg>-u)\""
| search _raw="*-u*0*" ("*-o*" OR argv0="usermod")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, _raw
tuning_guidance: There is essentially no legitimate reason to create a second UID-0 account on a modern RHEL system; this should be a page-now alert with no standing allowlist beyond a documented, time-boxed exception.
investigation_steps: Identify auid (the real user behind the command, even via sudo).
Check /etc/passwd for all UID 0 entries on the host.
Check whether the same account name was created on other hosts (fleet persistence).
response_guidance: Delete the unauthorized account immediately, audit all activity performed under it, and treat the host as compromised pending investigation.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1098.007: Additional Local or Domain Groups

author: Threat Detection Library

title: wheel/sudo Group Membership Changed
description: Detects an account being added to the wheel (or distro-equivalent sudo) group, which on most RHEL sudoers configurations grants unrestricted sudo access. This is a direct privilege-escalation and persistence primitive.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: Watch on /etc/group captures the write; gpasswd/usermod -aG invocation captured via EXECVE.

detection_logic: Watches for writes to /etc/group and gpasswd/usermod invocations targeting the wheel group.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "a0=\"(?<argv0>[^\"]+)\""
| where match(argv0, "(?i)(gpasswd|usermod)")
| where match(_raw, "wheel")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, _raw
tuning_guidance: Legitimate onboarding of a new administrator will trigger this; require correlation with a change ticket or an AAP/Satellite-driven provisioning job (RH-X-002) before treating as benign.
investigation_steps: Identify auid and the target account added.
Check whether the change is tied to a documented onboarding/access request.
Check whether the same account gained wheel membership on multiple hosts (fleet privilege expansion).
response_guidance: Revert unauthorized membership immediately and investigate the actor account for compromise.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1098.007: Additional Local or Domain Groups

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Password Aging/Complexity Weakened for an Account
description: Detects use of `chage` to remove password expiry (-M -1 / -E -1) or otherwise weaken password aging for an account, which attackers use to ensure a compromised or planted credential never expires and never forces a password change that would lock them out.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: chage invocation captured via EXECVE.

detection_logic: Matches EXECVE records for chage with flags that disable expiry or set a very large max-age.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "a0=\"(?<argv0>[^\"]+)\""
| where argv0="chage" AND match(_raw, "(-M -1|-M 99999|-E -1)")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| rex field=_raw "a\d=\"(?<target_user>[^\"\-][^\"]*)\"\s*$"
| table _time, host, auid, target_user, _raw
tuning_guidance: Some legitimate service accounts are intentionally configured with non-expiring passwords at provisioning time; suppress for accounts already on an approved non-expiring list and alert only on changes to previously-expiring accounts.
investigation_steps: Identify auid and the target account.
Check whether the account was recently created or recently authenticated from an unusual source.
Cross-reference with account-creation detections for the same account.
response_guidance: Revert the aging policy and investigate whether the account is otherwise compromised.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1556: Modify Authentication Process

author: Threat Detection Library

title: SSH authorized_keys Created or Modified
description: Detects creation or modification of any user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file. This is the most common SSH persistence mechanism: an attacker with any code-execution foothold appends their own public key to gain passwordless, durable access that survives password rotation.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: auditd watch on authorized_keys paths (requires a watch per home directory, or a broader watch on /home and /root).

detection_logic: Surfaces PATH/SYSCALL events for writes matching '.ssh/authorized_keys' anywhere under /home or /root, along with the writing process and real user.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=PATH path="*.ssh/authorized_keys*"
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| rex field=_raw "exe=\"(?<exe>[^\"]+)\""
| table _time, host, auid, exe, path
tuning_guidance: Configuration management (Ansible authorized_key module, cloud-init, Satellite provisioning) legitimately manages these files; correlate with AAP job execution (RH-X-003) and exclude the known management process (e.g. ansible's atomic-move temp-file pattern) rather than the path itself.
investigation_steps: Diff the file against the previous version to see the added key.
Identify auid/exe - human shell vs. configuration management.
Check whether the same key was added to authorized_keys on other hosts (fleet persistence, RH-X pattern).
response_guidance: Remove any unauthorized key immediately, audit all sessions that authenticated with it, and rotate affected credentials.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1098.004: SSH Authorized Keys

author: Threat Detection Library

title: sshd_config Modified
description: Detects modification of /etc/ssh/sshd_config or /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/. Attackers modify sshd's own configuration to weaken authentication requirements (enable PermitRootLogin, enable PasswordAuthentication, widen AllowUsers/AllowGroups) as a durable access-broadening step.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: Write watch on sshd_config and its include directory.

detection_logic: Surfaces writes to the sshd configuration path; a follow-on correlation checks for an sshd reload/restart shortly after (RHEL-019), which confirms the change was activated.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=PATH (path="/etc/ssh/sshd_config" OR path="/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| rex field=_raw "exe=\"(?<exe>[^\"]+)\""
| table _time, host, auid, exe, path
tuning_guidance: Configuration management-driven hardening changes are expected periodically; correlate against AAP/Satellite job execution and package updates (openssh-server RPM updates touch this file) before escalating.
investigation_steps: Diff the configuration for PermitRootLogin, PasswordAuthentication, and AllowUsers/AllowGroups changes specifically.
Identify auid/exe.
Check for a subsequent sshd restart/reload and any new SSH sessions immediately after.
response_guidance: Revert to the known-good configuration via configuration management and investigate the actor.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1556: Modify Authentication Process

author: Threat Detection Library

title: sshd Restarted Shortly After Configuration Change
description: Detects sshd being restarted or reloaded within minutes of its configuration file changing, confirming that a modification (RHEL-018) was actually activated rather than sitting unapplied. This closes the loop between 'file was written' and 'the new behavior is now live.'

data_sources.name: systemd (journald)
data_sources.description: systemd service start/reload events for sshd.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: sshd_config write events.

detection_logic: Joins an sshd_config write event to a subsequent sshd unit restart/reload within a short window.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=PATH path="/etc/ssh/sshd_config*"
| rename _time as config_change_time
| join type=inner host
    [ search index=linux sourcetype=systemd_journal unit=sshd (action=restart OR action=reload)
      | rename _time as restart_time ]
| eval delta_seconds=restart_time-config_change_time
| where delta_seconds >= 0 AND delta_seconds <= 300
| table config_change_time, restart_time, host, delta_seconds
tuning_guidance: Configuration management runs typically do this as an atomic step (write, then reload) as part of normal operation; the value here is in confirming activation, and severity should be driven primarily by whether the underlying change (RHEL-018) itself was authorized.
investigation_steps: Review exactly what changed in sshd_config.
Check for new SSH sessions immediately following the restart.
Confirm the restart was triggered by configuration management, not manually.
response_guidance: If the underlying change was unauthorized, this confirms it is live - treat as urgent and revert immediately.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1556: Modify Authentication Process

author: Threat Detection Library

title: SSH Host Key Replaced
description: Detects regeneration/replacement of the host's SSH host keys (/etc/ssh/ssh_host_*_key). Legitimate only during initial provisioning or a deliberate rotation; unexpected replacement can indicate an attacker attempting to facilitate an SSH MITM or simply covering evidence of a prior unauthorized host-key change.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: Write watch on /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*.

detection_logic: Surfaces writes to host key material paths outside of a known provisioning window.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=PATH path="/etc/ssh/ssh_host_*"
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, path
tuning_guidance: Initial provisioning (cloud-init, kickstart) and documented key-rotation maintenance are the only expected sources; suppress during the provisioning window for newly-built hosts.
investigation_steps: Confirm whether the host was recently provisioned or is in a documented rotation window.
Check client-side known_hosts warnings reported by users connecting to this host.
Review who/what triggered the regeneration.
response_guidance: If unexpected, investigate for host compromise and notify users to verify the new host key fingerprint out-of-band.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1553: Subvert Trust Controls

author: Threat Detection Library

title: New setuid/setgid Binary Created
description: Detects a chmod/chown operation that sets the setuid or setgid bit on a binary outside of package management. A setuid-root binary planted by an attacker (or a legitimate binary re-permissioned) runs with root privileges regardless of the invoking user, making it a durable local-privilege-escalation primitive.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: chmod/fchmodat syscalls with mode bits 4000/2000 set.

detection_logic: Matches SYSCALL records for chmod-family syscalls where the mode argument includes the setuid (04000) or setgid (02000) bit, outside of an RPM transaction.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=SYSCALL (syscall=chmod OR syscall=fchmodat OR syscall=fchmod)
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| rex field=_raw "a1=(?<mode_hex>[0-9a-f]+)"
| eval mode_dec=tonumber(mode_hex,16)
| where (mode_dec % 8192) >= 4096 OR (mode_dec % 4096) >= 2048
| lookup rpm_transaction_window.csv host OUTPUT in_rpm_transaction
| where isnull(in_rpm_transaction)
| table _time, host, auid, mode_hex
tuning_guidance: Package installs/updates that ship setuid binaries (sudo, passwd, ping) are the primary legitimate source; exclude activity that falls inside an active dnf/rpm transaction window.
investigation_steps: Identify the specific file path (correlate the matching PATH record) and whether it is a known system binary or something new.
Identify auid.
Check the binary's hash/provenance against the RPM database (`rpm -qf <path>`).
response_guidance: Remove the setuid/setgid bit or the file entirely if unauthorized, and investigate how it was introduced.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1548.001: Setuid and Setgid

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Linux Capability Granted to a File
description: Detects use of `setcap` to grant a Linux capability (e.g. cap_setuid, cap_net_raw, cap_sys_admin) to a file. File capabilities are a setuid-bit alternative attackers use to grant a binary powerful kernel privileges without the more commonly-monitored setuid bit.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: setcap invocation captured via EXECVE.

detection_logic: Matches EXECVE records for the setcap binary.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "a0=\"(?<argv0>[^\"]+)\""
| where argv0="setcap"
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, _raw
tuning_guidance: A small, well-known set of system binaries (ping, some container runtimes) legitimately use file capabilities; maintain an allowlist of expected path/capability pairs.
investigation_steps: Identify the target file and capability granted.
Check whether the capability (especially cap_setuid, cap_sys_admin, cap_sys_ptrace) allows privilege escalation.
Identify auid.
response_guidance: Remove the capability if unauthorized (`setcap -r`) and investigate the actor.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1548: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism

author: Threat Detection Library

title: pkexec / polkit Privilege Escalation Activity
description: Detects execution of `pkexec` (Polkit's setuid-root helper) especially with anomalous arguments or immediately following authentication failures, which can indicate exploitation attempts against Polkit privilege-escalation vulnerabilities (a recurring CVE class, e.g. CVE-2021-4034 'PwnKit') as well as ordinary abuse of overly-permissive Polkit rules.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: pkexec invocation via EXECVE; polkitd authorization log.

detection_logic: Surfaces pkexec invocations, with special attention to zero/missing-argument invocations (a signature of several public PwnKit-style exploits) or invocations from an unusual parent process.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "a0=\"(?<argv0>[^\"]+)\""
| where argv0="pkexec"
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| rex field=_raw "argc=(?<argc>\d+)"
| eval suspicious=if(argc<=1,1,0)
| table _time, host, auid, argc, suspicious, _raw
tuning_guidance: GUI-driven administrative actions (GNOME Settings, package managers with a polkit-backed GUI) legitimately invoke pkexec with normal arguments; the argc<=1 pattern specifically has very low legitimate incidence and should be treated with elevated confidence.
investigation_steps: Check the RHEL minor version/pkexec package version against known CVEs.
Identify auid and parent process.
Check for a resulting root shell/process spawned by pkexec.
response_guidance: If exploitation is suspected, isolate the host, patch polkit immediately, and treat as a confirmed privilege-escalation incident.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1548: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism

author: Threat Detection Library

title: World-Writable File Referenced by a Privileged Service or Cron Job
description: Detects a systemd service, cron job, or PATH-referenced script that points at a world-writable file. Any low-privilege user can overwrite such a file to have their code executed the next time the privileged job/service runs, a classic Linux privilege-escalation-via-writable-script pattern.

techniques.name: Path Interception by PATH Environment Variable

data_sources.name: File integrity / configuration scan
data_sources.description: Requires a periodic scan correlating systemd ExecStart= and crontab command paths against filesystem permissions (not a real-time log source).

detection_logic: This is a configuration-scan detection rather than a log-based one: enumerate ExecStart= paths from systemd units and command paths from crontab/cron.d, stat() each for world-writable permissions, and index the results for Splunk to alert on.
spl:
`comment("Requires a scheduled scan feeding results into Splunk via HEC or a lookup-backed report")`
index=linux sourcetype=config_scan:writable_privileged_scripts world_writable=true
| table _time, host, service_or_job, script_path, owner, permissions
tuning_guidance: This class of finding is almost always a genuine hardening gap rather than active exploitation in progress; treat as a vulnerability-management finding with a shorter remediation SLA rather than a real-time SOC page, unless correlated with actual unexpected file modification.
investigation_steps: Identify who/what can write to the referenced path.
Check file modification history for unexpected recent changes.
Determine the privilege level the referencing service/job runs as.
response_guidance: Tighten permissions on the referenced script immediately; treat as higher urgency if file content shows signs of tampering.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1574.007: Path Interception by PATH Environment Variable

author: Threat Detection Library

title: auditd Service Stopped or Failed
description: Detects the auditd service being stopped, disabled, or failing. auditd is the source of truth for a large fraction of this catalogue's RHEL detections (EXECVE, PATH, account changes); its loss creates a substantial blind spot and is a common early step for an attacker seeking to operate without leaving an audit trail.

techniques.name: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System Log

data_sources.name: systemd (journald)
data_sources.description: systemd service state-change events for the auditd unit.

data_sources.name: auditd (self-reported)
data_sources.description: The final events auditd writes before stopping, including SERVICE_STOP.

detection_logic: This detection must correlate two sources because auditd cannot log its own absence indefinitely: a systemd SERVICE_STOP/failed event for the auditd unit, cross-checked against a subsequent gap in audit.log ingestion for that host.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=SERVICE_STOP unit=auditd
| table _time, host

`comment("Companion absence-of-telemetry check")`
| tstats latest(_time) as last_seen from index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit by host
| eval minutes_since=round((now()-last_seen)/60,1)
| where minutes_since > 15
tuning_guidance: Legitimate maintenance (auditd package upgrade, planned reconfiguration requiring a restart) briefly stops the service; correlate with a change ticket or AAP job execution, and expect the service to be back within seconds to a few minutes, not indefinitely.
investigation_steps: Identify who/what stopped the service (check the last commands executed before the stop, if still available in the buffer).
Check whether SELinux/fapolicyd/firewalld were also impaired around the same time (fleet defense-evasion pattern, RH-X-010).
Confirm the service was restarted and confirm audit rules are intact afterward.
response_guidance: Restart auditd immediately, verify -e 2 immutable mode and rule integrity, and treat the host as compromised if the stop cannot be attributed to authorized maintenance.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1685.004: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System Log

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Audit Rules Modified or Deleted (auditctl -D)
description: Detects use of `auditctl -D` (delete all rules) or removal of specific watches/rules, which silently narrows or eliminates audit visibility while leaving the auditd process itself running - a stealthier alternative to stopping the service outright, since a superficial 'is auditd running?' check would not catch it.

techniques.name: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System Log

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: CONFIG_CHANGE events are emitted by the kernel audit subsystem itself whenever rules change, making this hard for an attacker to suppress without disabling audit entirely.

detection_logic: Filters CONFIG_CHANGE audit records for rule-deletion operations (op=remove_rule) or a bulk delete-all event.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=CONFIG_CHANGE (op="remove_rule" OR _raw="*audit_backlog*" OR _raw="*auid*rule*deleted*")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, _raw
tuning_guidance: Configuration management occasionally reloads the full ruleset (implemented as delete-all then reapply) as part of a normal audit.rules deployment; this should complete in well under a second and re-establish the full expected rule count immediately - a deletion with no prompt reload is the actionable case.
investigation_steps: Check whether the rule count returned to the expected baseline within seconds (`auditctl -l` count).
Identify auid.
Check for other defense-impairment activity in the same session.
response_guidance: Reapply the audit ruleset immediately (RHEL Hardening Monitoring Pack) and treat the host as compromised if the deletion was not immediately followed by a legitimate reload.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1685.004: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System Log

author: Threat Detection Library
audit_rules: -e 2  ; # make the ruleset immutable until reboot once deployed, per the Required RHEL Audit Policy

title: Audit Log Files Deleted or Truncated
description: Detects deletion or truncation of files under /var/log/audit/, removing historical evidence of prior activity even if auditd itself remains running and correctly configured going forward.

techniques.name: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: A watch on the audit log directory itself, plus SERVICE_START events for auditd showing the log was reinitialized.

detection_logic: Watches for unlink/truncate/rename syscalls targeting /var/log/audit/*, and separately for the file size of the active audit.log dropping to near-zero between consecutive checks.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=SYSCALL (syscall=unlink OR syscall=unlinkat OR syscall=truncate OR syscall=rename)
| search _raw="*audit.log*" OR _raw="*/var/log/audit/*"
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, syscall
tuning_guidance: Log rotation (logrotate) legitimately renames/compresses audit.log on a schedule via a documented process; exclude the logrotate process itself and its expected schedule.
investigation_steps: Identify auid and the process performing the deletion.
Check whether this coincides with the audit rules being deleted (RHEL-026) or auditd being stopped (RHEL-025).
Check for available backups/forwarded copies of the deleted logs (if forwarding to Splunk was already in place, the forwarded copy is unaffected).
response_guidance: Treat as a high-confidence anti-forensics indicator; preserve any forwarded/replicated copies immediately and begin incident response.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1685.006: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Audit Backlog Overflow / Lost Events
description: Detects the kernel audit subsystem reporting a backlog overflow or lost events, which is either an under-provisioned audit backlog (operational issue) or a deliberate flood of noisy audit-generating activity used to push meaningful events out of a limited backlog before they can be read/forwarded.

techniques.name: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System Log

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: Kernel-level audit backlog-limit and lost-event counters logged by the audit subsystem.

detection_logic: Matches kernel audit messages reporting backlog_wait_time exceeded or audit: lost N events.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit (_raw="*audit: backlog limit exceeded*" OR _raw="*audit: rate limit exceeded*" OR _raw="*audit_lost*")
| rex field=_raw "audit_lost=(?<lost_count>\d+)"
| table _time, host, lost_count, _raw
tuning_guidance: A host under genuine heavy load (bulk package install, large compilation job) can transiently hit backlog limits; treat isolated single occurrences as operational and escalate on repeated/sustained loss.
investigation_steps: Check what process(es) were generating high audit event volume at the time.
Check backlog_limit and rate_limit settings in auditd.conf against best-practice minimums.
Cross-reference the gap window for other suspicious activity that may have been intentionally obscured.
response_guidance: Increase the audit backlog limit per the Required RHEL Audit Policy and investigate the source of the event flood if it appears deliberate.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1685.004: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System Log

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Audit Log File Permissions Weakened
description: Detects a chmod/chown on /var/log/audit/ or its contents that widens read/write access beyond the default root-only permissions, which can allow a non-root process to read sensitive audit data or, worse, tamper with it directly.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: chmod/chown syscalls targeting the audit log directory.

detection_logic: Matches SYSCALL records for chmod/chown against paths under /var/log/audit/.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=SYSCALL (syscall=chmod OR syscall=chown OR syscall=fchmodat OR syscall=fchownat)
| search key="audit_log_protection"
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, syscall
tuning_guidance: This path should never need permission changes outside of the initial OS build/hardening baseline; any occurrence in steady state warrants investigation.
investigation_steps: Check the resulting permissions on the audit log directory.
Identify auid.
Restore correct permissions (0600 for audit.log, 0750 for the directory) immediately.
response_guidance: Revert permissions and treat as a probable precursor to audit-log tampering; investigate for related activity.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1222.002: Linux and Mac Permissions

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Audit Watch Removed for a Previously Monitored Path
description: Detects a specific audit watch (e.g. on /etc/sudoers, /etc/passwd, or an authorized_keys path) disappearing from the active ruleset without a corresponding full rule reload, indicating an attacker with root access selectively blinding audit coverage for the exact path they intend to modify next.

techniques.name: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System Log

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: CONFIG_CHANGE op=remove_rule events, compared against the expected ruleset baseline.

detection_logic: Compares the currently active rule keys (from CONFIG_CHANGE add/remove events) against the Required RHEL Audit Policy baseline key list; flags any expected key missing after a remove event with no matching re-add.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=CONFIG_CHANGE op="remove_rule"
| rex field=_raw "key=\"(?<key>[^\"]+)\""
| lookup required_audit_policy_keys.csv key OUTPUT is_required_key
| where is_required_key=1
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, key
tuning_guidance: A full, intentional ruleset redeployment removes and re-adds all keys together in quick succession; this detection's value is in catching a single key vanishing while the rest of the ruleset remains intact.
investigation_steps: Confirm which specific watch was removed and what it covered.
Check for activity on that exact path immediately after removal.
Identify auid.
response_guidance: Reapply the missing rule immediately and treat any subsequent activity on the now-unwatched path with elevated suspicion.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1685.004: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System Log

author: Threat Detection Library

title: SELinux Disabled or Set to Permissive
description: Detects SELinux being set to permissive or disabled via `setenforce 0` or a change to /etc/selinux/config. Permissive mode logs but no longer enforces SELinux policy, silently removing a major layer of confinement (e.g. against web-shell-to-root escapes) while `sestatus` casually reviewed by an admin can still show 'SELinux status: enabled' if only the mode changed.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: setenforce invocation via EXECVE, and MAC_STATUS records emitted by the kernel on enforcement-mode change.

detection_logic: Matches MAC_STATUS audit records (emitted directly by the kernel whenever enforcement mode changes, independent of which tool made the change) and setenforce EXECVE invocations.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit (type=MAC_STATUS OR (type=EXECVE _raw="*setenforce*"))
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| rex field=_raw "enforcing=(?<enforcing>\d)"
| where enforcing=0 OR match(_raw,"setenforce\s+0")
| table _time, host, auid, _raw
tuning_guidance: Some legitimate troubleshooting temporarily sets permissive mode to isolate whether SELinux is the cause of an application issue; this should always be brief, documented, and reverted - alert on the transition itself and separately verify enforcing mode is restored within an expected window.
investigation_steps: Confirm current mode with `getenforce`/`sestatus`.
Identify auid and whether a troubleshooting ticket exists.
Check for AVC denials immediately preceding the change (may indicate the attacker hit an SELinux block and disabled it to proceed) and for suspicious activity immediately after.
response_guidance: Re-enable enforcing mode immediately (`setenforce 1`) and update /etc/selinux/config to persist across reboot; investigate any activity that occurred while permissive.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1685: Disable or Modify Tools

author: Threat Detection Library

title: SELinux Policy Module Installed or Removed
description: Detects use of `semodule -i`/`semodule -r` to install or remove an SELinux policy module. Attackers with root access can load a custom, overly-permissive policy module that grants a specific malicious process an exception to normal confinement, which is far stealthier than disabling SELinux entirely.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: semodule invocation via EXECVE.

detection_logic: Matches EXECVE records for semodule with install/remove flags.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "a0=\"(?<argv0>[^\"]+)\""
| where argv0="semodule"
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| eval action=case(match(_raw,"-i "),"install", match(_raw,"-r "),"remove", 1=1,"other")
| table _time, host, auid, action, _raw
tuning_guidance: Package installs that ship their own SELinux policy module (many enterprise applications do) legitimately call semodule during postinstall scripts; correlate with an active RPM transaction or configuration-management job before escalating.
investigation_steps: Identify the module name and its declared permissions (`semodule -l`, then inspect the .pp module content if retrievable).
Identify auid.
Check whether the module grants broad/unusual access to a specific domain.
response_guidance: Remove unauthorized modules immediately and investigate the actor for further tampering.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1685: Disable or Modify Tools

author: Threat Detection Library

title: SELinux Boolean Changed (setsebool)
description: Detects use of `setsebool` to toggle an SELinux policy boolean, particularly ones that widen network or execution access for a confined domain (e.g. httpd_can_network_connect, httpd_execmem, nis_enabled). Individually narrower than disabling SELinux outright, but a favored technique to enable one specific exploit path (e.g. a web shell needing outbound network access).

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: setsebool invocation via EXECVE.

detection_logic: Matches EXECVE records for setsebool, extracting the boolean name and target value.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "a0=\"(?<argv0>[^\"]+)\""
| where argv0="setsebool"
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, _raw
tuning_guidance: Application installation runbooks legitimately toggle specific booleans (e.g. enabling httpd_can_network_connect for a proxying web app); maintain an allowlist of expected boolean/value pairs per host role.
investigation_steps: Identify which boolean changed and to what value.
Assess whether the change specifically enables a known-risky capability for a network-facing service.
Identify auid.
response_guidance: Revert the boolean if not matching an approved application-installation pattern.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1685: Disable or Modify Tools

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Burst of SELinux AVC Denials
description: Detects a sudden burst of SELinux AVC (Access Vector Cache) denials for a single process/domain, which can indicate an attacker's tooling repeatedly hitting SELinux confinement while probing for a working exploitation path, or a newly-planted piece of malware whose expected behavior was never accounted for by policy.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: AVC denial records include the source context (scontext), target context (tcontext), and the requested permission.

detection_logic: Counts AVC denial events per source-domain/comm pair in a rolling window; a healthy, well-tuned system produces very few denials in steady state, so a burst is anomalous by volume alone.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=AVC
| rex field=_raw "scontext=(?<scontext>\S+)"
| rex field=_raw "tcontext=(?<tcontext>\S+)"
| rex field=_raw "comm=\"(?<comm>[^\"]+)\""
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count as denials values(tcontext) as targets by _time, host, comm, scontext
| where denials >= 20
tuning_guidance: A newly-deployed application or a policy that was never fully tuned for a legitimate app is the most common source; this is genuinely high-noise and works best as a discovery/triage feed rather than a standalone page.
investigation_steps: Identify comm and scontext - is this a known application or something unfamiliar?
Review what permissions/targets are being denied for a pattern (e.g. repeated attempts to write to /etc, connect outbound, or ptrace another process).
Cross-reference with process creation telemetry for the denied comm.
response_guidance: If tied to a legitimate application, file a policy exception through proper SELinux policy development (audit2allow reviewed by a human, not blindly applied); if tied to unfamiliar software, investigate as potential malware confinement working as intended.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1082: System Information Discovery

author: Threat Detection Library

title: fapolicyd Service Stopped or Disabled
description: Detects the fapolicyd service being stopped or disabled. fapolicyd is an application allowlisting daemon that blocks execution of untrusted binaries/scripts; disabling it removes a primary control against exactly the kind of dropped-binary and script-based execution attackers rely on post-compromise.

data_sources.name: systemd (journald)
data_sources.description: systemd service state-change events for fapolicyd.

detection_logic: Matches systemd SERVICE_STOP/failed events for the fapolicyd unit.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=SERVICE_STOP unit=fapolicyd
| table _time, host
tuning_guidance: Rare, brief maintenance windows for fapolicyd rule updates are the only expected legitimate cause; correlate with change tickets and expect near-immediate restart.
investigation_steps: Identify who/what stopped the service.
Check for execution of previously-blocked binaries/scripts immediately after the stop.
Verify rule integrity once restarted.
response_guidance: Restart fapolicyd immediately and review execution activity that occurred while it was down.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1685: Disable or Modify Tools

author: Threat Detection Library

title: fapolicyd Trust Database Modified
description: Detects an addition to fapolicyd's trust database (`fapolicyd-cli --file add` or a change under /etc/fapolicyd/rules.d/ and the trust files under /etc/fapolicyd/trust.d/), which allows an attacker-controlled binary to be treated as trusted and permitted to execute despite not being installed via RPM.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: fapolicyd-cli invocation via EXECVE, plus writes to /etc/fapolicyd/.

detection_logic: Matches EXECVE for fapolicyd-cli trust-modifying subcommands and PATH writes under /etc/fapolicyd/.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit (type=PATH path="/etc/fapolicyd/*") OR (type=EXECVE _raw="*fapolicyd-cli*")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, _raw
tuning_guidance: Legitimate installation of unsigned/vendor-provided software that isn't RPM-packaged requires an explicit trust addition; require this to be tied to a documented software-approval process.
investigation_steps: Identify exactly which file/hash was added to trust.
Verify the added binary's provenance and hash against a known-good source.
Identify auid.
response_guidance: Remove the unauthorized trust entry and quarantine/investigate the referenced binary.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1553: Subvert Trust Controls

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Repeated fapolicyd Execution Denials
description: Detects repeated fapolicyd execution denials for the same or similar binaries, indicating an attacker's dropped tooling is being blocked and they are retrying (potentially with variants, different paths, or renamed copies) to find something that executes.

data_sources.name: fapolicyd (audit/syslog)
data_sources.description: fapolicyd logs each denied execution with the path, invoking user, and trigger rule.

detection_logic: Counts distinct denied executable paths attempted by a single user/session in a rolling window.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=fapolicyd_log decision=deny
| bin _time span=10m
| stats count as denials dc(path) as distinct_paths values(path) as attempted_paths by _time, host, user
| where denials >= 5
tuning_guidance: Developers legitimately running self-compiled tools on a workstation-like server, or a newly-onboarded application not yet added to trust, can trigger a handful of denials; distinguish by path pattern (attempts from /tmp, /dev/shm, /var/tmp are far higher confidence than a developer's home directory build output).
investigation_steps: Review the attempted paths for temp-directory or unusual-location execution attempts.
Identify the user/session and its authentication origin.
Check whether any attempt eventually succeeded (trust was added, or the file was moved to a trusted path).
response_guidance: Investigate the source of the denied binaries; if malicious, preserve a sample for analysis and investigate how it was delivered to the host.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Untrusted ELF Execution Attempt from /tmp or /dev/shm
description: Detects a specific, high-confidence fapolicyd denial: an attempt to execute an ELF binary from /tmp, /dev/shm, /var/tmp, or another world-writable location. These paths are the standard drop location for attacker tooling precisely because they are usually writable by any user; execution attempts from them are rarely, if ever, legitimate.

data_sources.name: fapolicyd (audit/syslog)
data_sources.description: fapolicyd denial record including the path and file type.

detection_logic: Filters fapolicyd deny events to paths under known world-writable directories, regardless of volume - a single occurrence is actionable.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=fapolicyd_log decision=deny (path="/tmp/*" OR path="/dev/shm/*" OR path="/var/tmp/*")
| table _time, host, user, path, rule
tuning_guidance: Extremely low false-positive rate; the only known legitimate pattern is some package post-install scripts briefly staging a helper binary in /tmp, which should already be covered by an RPM-transaction exclusion.
investigation_steps: Retrieve and analyze the blocked binary if still present on disk.
Identify how it was delivered (download, extracted from an archive, written by another process).
Check for interpreter-based execution attempts (python/perl/bash script in the same location) that might not trigger this specific ELF-focused rule.
response_guidance: Treat as a confirmed intrusion indicator; isolate the host and begin incident response.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Interpreter Executing an Untrusted Script (fapolicyd Bypass Pattern)
description: Detects an interpreter (python, perl, bash, php) being used to execute an untrusted script file - fapolicyd's default policy in many deployments trusts the interpreter binary itself (since it's RPM-installed) but does not extend that trust to arbitrary scripts passed to it, and attackers exploit this gap deliberately to run untrusted code via a trusted interpreter.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: EXECVE records showing an interpreter's arguments referencing a script path outside trusted locations.

detection_logic: Matches EXECVE records where argv0 is a known interpreter and a subsequent argument is a file path under a world-writable or otherwise untrusted directory.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "a0=\"(?<interpreter>[^\"]+)\""
| where match(interpreter, "(?i)(python[23]?|perl|php|bash|sh)$")
| rex field=_raw "a1=\"(?<script_path>[^\"]+)\""
| where match(script_path, "^(/tmp/|/dev/shm/|/var/tmp/)")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, interpreter, script_path
tuning_guidance: Legitimate ad-hoc scripting by developers on shared dev/test boxes is the main source; scope this detection to production-tier hosts where interpreter use is expected to be limited to application-owned, package-installed script paths.
investigation_steps: Retrieve and review the script content if still on disk.
Identify auid and the session's origin.
Check whether fapolicyd generated a corresponding denial for the interpreter's read of the script, if configured to do so.
response_guidance: Treat as a probable execution-control bypass; isolate and investigate the host.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: New systemd Service Unit Created
description: Detects creation of a new .service unit file under /etc/systemd/system/ or /usr/lib/systemd/system/. Attackers create a systemd service (often running as root, often set to start on boot) as a durable persistence mechanism that survives reboots and blends in among the dozens of legitimate services already on a typical RHEL host.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: Watch on systemd unit directories captures the file creation.

detection_logic: Watches for file-creation events under systemd unit search paths.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=PATH (path="/etc/systemd/system/*.service" OR path="/usr/lib/systemd/system/*.service") type=CREATE
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, path
tuning_guidance: Package installations and configuration-management-driven application deployment routinely add service units; correlate against RPM transactions and AAP/Satellite job execution before treating as suspicious.
investigation_steps: Read the unit's ExecStart= and User= to see what it runs and as whom.
Identify auid.
Check whether the unit was also enabled and started immediately (RHEL-041).
response_guidance: If unauthorized, stop and disable the unit, remove the file, and investigate what it executed while active.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: systemd Service Enabled and Started With a Suspicious ExecStart
description: Detects a systemd service being enabled and started whose ExecStart= line invokes a shell, an interpreter with an inline command, or a binary located in a world-writable directory - the systemd equivalent of a suspicious cron entry, and a common pattern for reverse-shell and C2-beacon persistence.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: systemctl enable/start invocation via EXECVE, correlated with the unit file content.

detection_logic: Correlates a systemctl enable/start command with the ExecStart= line read from the corresponding unit file, flagging shell/interpreter invocations or paths under /tmp, /dev/shm, /var/tmp.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "a0=\"(?<argv0>[^\"]+)\""
| where argv0="systemctl" AND match(_raw, "(enable|start)")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| rex field=_raw "a2=\"(?<unit>[^\"]+)\""
| lookup systemd_unit_content.csv unit OUTPUT exec_start
| where match(exec_start, "(?i)(/bin/(ba)?sh|/tmp/|/dev/shm/|/var/tmp/|curl|wget|python|perl)")
| table _time, host, auid, unit, exec_start
tuning_guidance: Some legitimate wrapper services intentionally launch a shell script as their ExecStart; scope the world-writable-path check as the highest-confidence signal and treat plain shell-script invocation from a package-managed path as lower priority.
investigation_steps: Read the full unit file and ExecStart command.
Identify auid.
Check the service's current running state and any child processes it has spawned.
response_guidance: Stop and disable the service immediately, remove the unit file, and investigate all activity performed by the service while it ran.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Security-Relevant systemd Service Stopped
description: Detects an explicit stop of a security-relevant systemd service - auditd, fapolicyd, firewalld, rsyslog, sssd - via systemctl. Complements the service-specific detections above by covering the common command pattern directly and any additional security services not otherwise individually monitored.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: systemctl stop invocation via EXECVE.

detection_logic: Matches systemctl stop/disable/mask invocations targeting a maintained list of security-relevant unit names.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "a0=\"(?<argv0>[^\"]+)\""
| where argv0="systemctl" AND match(_raw, "(stop|disable|mask)")
| rex field=_raw "a2=\"(?<unit>[^\"]+)\""
| where match(unit, "(?i)(auditd|fapolicyd|firewalld|rsyslog|sssd)")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, unit
tuning_guidance: Planned maintenance windows are the only expected source; correlate with change tickets and AAP job execution.
investigation_steps: Identify which service and auid.
Check for other security-control impairment in the same session (defense-evasion combo).
Confirm the service is restarted promptly.
response_guidance: Restart the service immediately if unauthorized and investigate the actor.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: New systemd Timer Created
description: Detects creation of a new .timer unit, the systemd-native equivalent of a cron job. Timers are less commonly reviewed by administrators than crontab and are a growing persistence-mechanism choice on modern RHEL.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: Watch on systemd unit directories for .timer file creation.

detection_logic: Watches for .timer file creation under systemd unit search paths.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=PATH path="*.timer" type=CREATE
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, path
tuning_guidance: Application packages that ship scheduled maintenance tasks (log cleanup, cache refresh) legitimately install timers; correlate with RPM transactions.
investigation_steps: Read the paired .service unit the timer triggers.
Identify auid.
Check the timer's schedule (OnCalendar/OnBootSec) for unusually frequent or oddly-specific execution.
response_guidance: Disable and remove the timer/service pair if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Crontab or /etc/cron.d Entry Added
description: Detects a new entry added to a user crontab, /etc/crontab, or /etc/cron.d/ - one of the oldest and still most common Linux persistence mechanisms. Root's crontab in particular grants a durable, recurring execution primitive.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: Writes to cron spool/config paths; crontab command invocation via EXECVE.

detection_logic: Watches writes to /var/spool/cron/, /etc/crontab, and /etc/cron.d/, and separately captures `crontab -e`/`crontab -l` command invocations for attribution.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=PATH (path="/var/spool/cron/*" OR path="/etc/crontab" OR path="/etc/cron.d/*")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, path
tuning_guidance: Configuration management routinely manages cron entries for legitimate scheduled jobs; correlate with AAP/Satellite job execution and known application maintenance cron entries.
investigation_steps: Read the new entry's command and schedule.
Identify auid.
Check for shell-metacharacter obfuscation (base64, curl|bash) in the command.
response_guidance: Remove the unauthorized entry and investigate the actor for further tampering.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: at Job Scheduled
description: Detects use of the `at` command to schedule a one-time deferred job. Attackers use `at` for short-delay execution (e.g. to survive a brief detection window, or to trigger a payload after they've disconnected) and it is far less commonly monitored than cron.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: at invocation via EXECVE; job spool writes under /var/spool/at/.

detection_logic: Matches EXECVE records for the at/atd binary and writes to the at spool directory.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit (type=EXECVE _raw="*/usr/bin/at*") OR (type=PATH path="/var/spool/at/*")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, _raw
tuning_guidance: `at` is rarely used in well-managed enterprise RHEL environments; many organizations disable it entirely via at.deny. Any use in an environment where it's not an established practice warrants review.
investigation_steps: Read the scheduled command content from the spool file if still present.
Identify auid.
Check whether the job has already executed and what it did.
response_guidance: Cancel the pending job (`atrm`) if unauthorized and investigate the actor.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Shell Profile/rc File Modified (bashrc, profile, rc.local)
description: Detects modification of shell initialization files (~/.bashrc, ~/.bash_profile, /etc/profile, /etc/profile.d/, /etc/rc.local) that execute automatically when a user logs in or the system boots. Attackers append malicious commands here for a persistence mechanism that fires on every login rather than continuously, evading process-monitoring tools that only alert on long-running unexpected processes.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: Writes to shell initialization file paths.

detection_logic: Watches writes to known shell/system initialization script paths.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=PATH (path="*/.bashrc" OR path="*/.bash_profile" OR path="/etc/profile" OR path="/etc/profile.d/*" OR path="/etc/rc.local" OR path="/etc/rc.d/rc.local")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, path
tuning_guidance: Configuration management managing environment variables (PATH, proxy settings) for a fleet legitimately touches /etc/profile.d/; per-user .bashrc edits by the account owner are common and low-risk unless the account itself is compromised.
investigation_steps: Diff the file for the added content.
Identify auid - is this the file owner or a different/root account editing another user's file (higher suspicion)?
Check for base64/obfuscated payloads or outbound network commands in the addition.
response_guidance: Remove the unauthorized addition and investigate how the modifying account obtained access.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1546.004: Unix Shell Configuration Modification

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Kernel Module Loaded
description: Detects a kernel module being loaded via insmod/modprobe, particularly one not present in the RPM package database. Kernel modules run with the highest privilege on the system and are the basis of most Linux rootkits (hiding processes, files, and network connections from userspace tools).

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: init_module/finit_module syscalls, and insmod/modprobe invocation via EXECVE.

detection_logic: Matches the init_module/finit_module syscalls the kernel emits for every module load, cross-referenced against a lookup of modules shipped by installed RPMs to flag unpackaged modules.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=SYSCALL (syscall=init_module OR syscall=finit_module)
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| rex field=_raw "exe=\"(?<exe>[^\"]+)\""
| lookup rpm_owned_kernel_modules.csv module_name OUTPUT is_rpm_owned
| where isnull(is_rpm_owned)
| table _time, host, auid, exe
tuning_guidance: Third-party hardware drivers (storage HBAs, GPU drivers) and DKMS-built modules are the main legitimate unpackaged-module source; maintain the RPM/DKMS-owned module lookup and refresh it after driver updates.
investigation_steps: Identify the module name and check whether it is signed.
Identify auid.
Check `lsmod` and kernel taint status (`cat /proc/sys/kernel/tainted`) for confirmation.
response_guidance: Unload the module if unauthorized (`rmmod`), and treat the host as potentially rootkitted - a full reinstall from known-good media is the only fully reliable remediation for a suspected kernel-level compromise.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1547.006: Kernel Modules and Extensions

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Unsigned Kernel Module Load Rejected / Kernel Taint Changed
description: Detects the kernel's tainted state changing (via /proc/sys/kernel/tainted or a corresponding audit/dmesg message) or an explicit module-signature verification failure, which indicates an unsigned or out-of-tree module was force-loaded (module signature enforcement bypassed), a strong rootkit indicator on a properly hardened RHEL host.

data_sources.name: auditd / dmesg
data_sources.description: Kernel taint flag changes and module signature verification failure messages.

detection_logic: Monitors for kernel log lines indicating a module load without a valid signature, or a change in the tainted bitmask that includes the 'module was force-loaded' or 'unsigned module was loaded' bits.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_messages_syslog (_raw="*module verification failed*" OR _raw="*loading out-of-tree module taints kernel*" OR _raw="*unsigned module*")
| table _time, host, _raw
tuning_guidance: Legitimate but unsigned third-party/DKMS drivers (some GPU and RAID controller vendors) can taint the kernel as a matter of course on certain hardware; this should be a known, documented, and rare baseline state per host model rather than something occurring newly on an already-running host.
investigation_steps: Check `cat /proc/sys/kernel/tainted` and decode the bitmask.
Identify which module caused the taint.
Compare against the host's documented hardware/driver baseline.
response_guidance: Treat an unexpected new taint on a previously-untainted host as a likely rootkit indicator; escalate to full forensic investigation and rebuild from known-good media.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1547.006: Kernel Modules and Extensions

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Security-Relevant sysctl Value Changed
description: Detects a change to a security-relevant kernel sysctl parameter, such as kernel.yama.ptrace_scope (controls which processes can ptrace others - a common credential-dumping/injection prerequisite), kernel.dmesg_restrict, kernel.kptr_restrict, or net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: sysctl invocation via EXECVE, or writes to /etc/sysctl.conf and /etc/sysctl.d/.

detection_logic: Matches EXECVE for sysctl -w against a maintained list of security-relevant parameters, and writes to sysctl configuration files.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "a0=\"(?<argv0>[^\"]+)\""
| where argv0="sysctl"
| where match(_raw, "(kernel.yama.ptrace_scope|kernel.dmesg_restrict|kernel.kptr_restrict|kernel.modules_disabled)")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, _raw
tuning_guidance: Some container/observability tooling legitimately requires ptrace_scope=0; scope hosts running such tooling into an allowlist rather than suppressing the detection globally.
investigation_steps: Identify which parameter changed and to what value.
Identify auid.
Assess the specific security implication (e.g. ptrace_scope=0 permits credential-dumping tools like a Mimikatz-equivalent to attach to arbitrary processes).
response_guidance: Revert to the hardened value unless an approved exception exists.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1685: Disable or Modify Tools

author: Threat Detection Library

title: bpftool / eBPF Program Loaded Outside Expected Tooling
description: Detects use of `bpftool` or a direct `bpf()` syscall (BPF_PROG_LOAD) to load an eBPF program outside of known observability/security tooling (e.g. Falco, Cilium, approved APM agents). eBPF-based rootkits and covert packet-capture/keylogging tools are an emerging Linux threat class precisely because eBPF programs run in the kernel and can hook syscalls, network traffic, and file I/O with capabilities that rival a traditional kernel-module rootkit while being harder for defenders to enumerate.

data_sources.name: auditd
