data_sources.description: bpf() syscall with cmd=BPF_PROG_LOAD; bpftool invocation via EXECVE.

detection_logic: Matches bpf() syscalls with the program-load command, or bpftool prog load invocations, and excludes processes matching a maintained allowlist of approved eBPF-consuming tools.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=SYSCALL syscall=bpf
| rex field=_raw "exe=\"(?<exe>[^\"]+)\""
| lookup approved_ebpf_tools.csv exe OUTPUT is_approved
| where isnull(is_approved)
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, exe
tuning_guidance: This requires maintaining an accurate allowlist of every legitimate eBPF-consuming agent in the environment (APM, CNI, security tooling); expect meaningful tuning effort during rollout, and start in monitor-only mode.
investigation_steps: Identify the loading process/binary and its origin.
Check what BPF program type was loaded (tracing, XDP, socket filter) if extractable.
Check for unusual network capture or syscall-hooking behavior on the host afterward.
response_guidance: Investigate the process for legitimacy; if unauthorized, treat as a likely rootkit/implant and begin incident response - eBPF-based implants often survive normal process-kill and require kernel-level cleanup or a reboot.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: firewalld Disabled or Flushed
description: Detects firewalld being stopped/disabled, or its runtime ruleset being flushed via nft/iptables directly (bypassing firewalld's own configuration), removing host-level network filtering and potentially exposing services that were only intended to be reachable after filtering.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: systemctl stop firewalld via EXECVE; nft/iptables flush commands.

detection_logic: Matches systemctl stop/disable for firewalld and nft/iptables flush-all invocations.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "a0=\"(?<argv0>[^\"]+)\""
| where (argv0="systemctl" AND match(_raw,"firewalld") AND match(_raw,"(stop|disable)")) OR (argv0="nft" AND match(_raw,"flush ruleset")) OR (argv0="iptables" AND match(_raw,"-F"))
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, _raw
tuning_guidance: Planned network reconfiguration or a documented migration to a different filtering approach (e.g. moving to a centrally-managed nftables ruleset) can trigger this legitimately; correlate with change tickets.
investigation_steps: Identify auid.
Check the resulting firewall state and any newly-reachable listening services.
Check for new inbound connections immediately after the change.
response_guidance: Restore firewall rules immediately and investigate the actor.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1686: Disable or Modify System Firewall

author: Threat Detection Library

title: New Listening Service Bound to a Network Socket
description: Detects a process binding to a new listening TCP/UDP port not previously observed on the host, which can indicate a planted backdoor listener, an unauthorized service, or a C2 implant awaiting inbound connections.

data_sources.name: Network telemetry / auditd
data_sources.path: n/a - requires periodic ss/netstat snapshot or auditd bind() syscall watch
data_sources.description: A scheduled scan comparing the current listening-socket table against a maintained baseline per host.

detection_logic: Baseline-oriented: a scheduled script snapshots `ss -tlnp` output, indexes it, and Splunk compares against a per-host baseline lookup of expected listening ports.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=listening_ports_scan
| lookup expected_listening_ports.csv host, port OUTPUT is_expected
| where isnull(is_expected)
| table _time, host, port, process, pid
tuning_guidance: Application deployments and version upgrades that change a listening port are the primary source; refresh the baseline lookup as part of the deployment pipeline (ideally auto-updated by AAP/Satellite job completion).
investigation_steps: Identify the process and its binary path/hash.
Check whether the port matches a known application's documented port.
Check for inbound connections to the new port.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, kill the process, remove its persistence mechanism, and block the port at the host firewall pending investigation.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1071: Application Layer Protocol

author: Threat Detection Library

title: IP Forwarding Enabled
description: Detects net.ipv4.ip_forward (or the IPv6 equivalent) being enabled on a host that is not a designated router/gateway. Attackers enable IP forwarding to turn a compromised host into a pivot point, routing traffic into segments it would not otherwise be able to reach directly.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: sysctl invocation or direct write to /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward.

detection_logic: Matches sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 (and IPv6 equivalent) invocations, scoped to hosts not tagged as approved routers/gateways.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE _raw="*ip_forward=1*"
| lookup approved_gateway_hosts.csv host OUTPUT is_gateway
| where isnull(is_gateway)
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid
tuning_guidance: Legitimate container/VPN/gateway hosts require this permanently; maintain the approved-gateway host list and alert only on unexpected hosts.
investigation_steps: Identify auid and why forwarding was enabled.
Check for new proxy/routing configuration (nft/iptables NAT rules) added around the same time.
Check for unusual cross-segment traffic sourced from or through the host.
response_guidance: Disable IP forwarding if unauthorized and investigate the host for a pivot/proxy setup.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DNS Resolver Configuration Changed
description: Detects modification of /etc/resolv.conf or NetworkManager DNS settings to point at a DNS server outside the approved corporate resolver list, which can be used to redirect name resolution toward attacker-controlled infrastructure for C2 or to serve poisoned responses for internal hostnames.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: Writes to /etc/resolv.conf and NetworkManager connection profiles.

detection_logic: Watches writes to resolv.conf and NetworkManager DNS-related keyfiles, joined against a lookup of approved resolver IPs to flag unapproved values where extractable.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=PATH (path="/etc/resolv.conf" OR path="/etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/*")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, path
tuning_guidance: DHCP-driven resolver updates and legitimate network changes occur regularly; this is most valuable when correlated with the actual resolver IP against an approved allowlist rather than alerting on every write.
investigation_steps: Extract the new resolver IP(s) and compare against approved corporate resolvers.
Identify auid.
Check subsequent DNS query patterns for the host if DNS telemetry is available.
response_guidance: Revert to approved resolvers if unauthorized and investigate the host for compromise.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Download-and-Execute Pattern (curl/wget piped to shell)
description: Detects the classic `curl <url> | bash` (or wget equivalent) pattern: downloading a remote script and piping it directly to an interpreter without ever writing it to disk for review. This is one of the highest-confidence single-line indicators of malware staging/installation on Linux, since it is functionally never necessary for legitimate configuration-managed software delivery.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: EXECVE records for curl/wget and the piped-to shell, correlated by parent-child process relationship or shell command-line reconstruction.

detection_logic: Reconstructs the shell command line from EXECVE argv records and matches the pipe-to-interpreter pattern directly, which is more reliable than trying to correlate separate curl and bash EXECVE events.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "a0=\"(?<argv0>[^\"]+)\""
| where match(argv0, "(?i)(bash|sh|dash)$")
| rex field=_raw "a2=\"(?<cmdline>[^\"]+)\""
| where match(cmdline, "(?i)(curl|wget).*\|\s*(ba)?sh")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, cmdline
tuning_guidance: A small number of vendor-published install scripts (some language version managers, some cloud CLI installers) document this exact pattern; maintain a narrow allowlist of specific approved install URLs rather than suppressing the pattern broadly.
investigation_steps: Retrieve the source URL and, if still reachable, fetch and review the script content.
Identify auid and the session origin.
Check what the piped script actually executed (subsequent EXECVE events from the same shell).
response_guidance: Treat as a high-confidence intrusion indicator pending confirmation of an approved installer; isolate the host and investigate.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1105: Ingress Tool Transfer

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Base64-Decode Piped to Shell Execution
description: Detects a command line that base64-decodes a string or file and pipes the result directly into a shell for execution - a common technique to smuggle an encoded payload past simple string-matching defenses and into memory without writing a plaintext script to disk.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: Reconstructed shell command line via EXECVE.

detection_logic: Matches command lines containing 'base64 -d' or 'base64 --decode' piped into a shell interpreter.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "a2=\"(?<cmdline>[^\"]+)\""
| where match(cmdline, "(?i)base64\s+(-d|--decode).*\|\s*(ba)?sh")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, cmdline
tuning_guidance: Very low legitimate incidence; some CI/CD secret-injection patterns decode a base64 credential, but piping the *decoded output itself* into a shell for execution has essentially no legitimate use case.
investigation_steps: Attempt to recover and decode the original base64 string from process arguments/history if still available.
Identify auid.
Analyze the decoded payload for further IOCs.
response_guidance: Treat as a confirmed intrusion indicator; isolate the host and begin incident response.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1140: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Reverse Shell Pattern via nc/socat/bash
description: Detects command-line patterns characteristic of a reverse or bind shell: `nc -e /bin/sh`, `bash -i >& /dev/tcp/...`, or `socat exec:`. These are among the most well-known post-exploitation one-liners and have essentially zero legitimate administrative use in a managed enterprise environment.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: Reconstructed shell command line via EXECVE.

detection_logic: Matches well-known reverse/bind-shell one-liner signatures against reconstructed command lines.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "a2=\"(?<cmdline>[^\"]+)\""
| where match(cmdline, "(?i)(nc(at)?\s+-e\s|/dev/tcp/|socat\s+.*exec:|bash\s+-i\s*>&)")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, cmdline
tuning_guidance: Essentially no legitimate false-positive source in a standard enterprise environment; penetration-testing engagements are the only known exception and should be explicitly scheduled and allowlisted for their duration.
investigation_steps: Identify the destination IP/port from the command.
Identify auid and the process tree leading to this command.
Check network telemetry for an established outbound connection to the target.
response_guidance: Treat as an active, ongoing compromise; isolate the host from the network immediately and begin incident response.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1071: Application Layer Protocol

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Archive Creation Followed by Outbound Transfer
description: Detects a tar/zip/gzip archive-creation command followed shortly by a network-transfer command (scp, sftp, curl -T, rsync to an external host) from the same session - the classic stage-then-exfiltrate pattern.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: EXECVE records for archive tools and transfer tools, correlated by session (ses) within a short window.

detection_logic: Joins an archive-creation EXECVE event to a transfer-tool EXECVE event referencing the same file path (or the same audit session ID) within a short window.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "a0=\"(?<argv0>[^\"]+)\""
| rex field=_raw "ses=(?<ses>\d+)"
| eval action=case(match(argv0,"(?i)(tar|zip|gzip)"),"archive", match(argv0,"(?i)(scp|sftp|rsync|curl)"),"transfer", 1=1,"")
| where action!=""
| stats values(action) as actions, values(argv0) as tools by host, ses
| where mvcount(actions)>1 AND mvfind(actions,"archive")>=0 AND mvfind(actions,"transfer")>=0
tuning_guidance: Legitimate backup jobs perform exactly this sequence; scope out known backup service accounts and their documented destinations, and pay closer attention to the same pattern from an interactive human session.
investigation_steps: Identify what was archived (sensitive data, credentials, configuration).
Identify the transfer destination and whether it's an approved backup target.
Identify auid/ses.
response_guidance: If the destination is not an approved backup/replication target, treat as a confirmed exfiltration event and begin incident response.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1560.001: Archive via Utility
MITRE ATT&CK T1048: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Read Access to /etc/shadow Outside Expected Processes
description: Detects a process other than the well-known small set that legitimately needs it (passwd, useradd family, PAM/SSSD, authconfig) opening /etc/shadow for read. The shadow file contains password hashes for every local account and is a primary target for offline password cracking once an attacker has any read access.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: open/openat syscalls against /etc/shadow.

detection_logic: Matches read-mode opens of /etc/shadow, excluding a maintained allowlist of expected system binaries.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=SYSCALL (syscall=open OR syscall=openat) key="shadow_access"
| rex field=_raw "exe=\"(?<exe>[^\"]+)\""
| lookup shadow_read_allowlist.csv exe OUTPUT is_allowed
| where isnull(is_allowed)
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, exe
tuning_guidance: Backup software that performs a full filesystem backup will legitimately read this file; exclude known backup agents explicitly by binary path/hash.
investigation_steps: Identify the reading process and its full command line.
Identify auid.
Check whether the file was subsequently copied/exfiltrated.
response_guidance: Rotate all local account passwords on the host as a precaution and investigate the reading process.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Bash History Accessed by a Process Other Than the Owning Shell
description: Detects a process reading another user's ~/.bash_history file, which attackers do to harvest credentials, internal hostnames, or command patterns that a careless user may have typed directly (e.g. `mysql -u root -pPassword123`).

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: open/openat syscalls against *.bash_history paths.

detection_logic: Matches reads of bash_history files where the reading process's real user (auid) does not own the home directory being read.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=SYSCALL (syscall=open OR syscall=openat) key="bash_history_access"
| rex field=_raw "exe=\"(?<exe>[^\"]+)\""
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| rex field=_raw "path=\"(?<target_path>[^\"]+bash_history)\""
| where NOT match(target_path, "^/home/".auid)
| table _time, host, auid, exe, target_path
tuning_guidance: Log-aggregation/backup agents reading all home directories indiscriminately are a common false-positive source; exclude by binary.
investigation_steps: Identify the reading process and auid.
Check whether any credentials appear in the target user's actual history (and rotate them proactively regardless of confirmed access).
Correlate with other credential-access indicators from the same session.
response_guidance: Advise the affected user to rotate any credentials that may have been typed in cleartext, and investigate the accessing account.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: SSH Private Key Accessed Outside Its Owning User
description: Detects a process reading another user's private SSH key material (~/.ssh/id_rsa, id_ed25519, etc.), which an attacker does to harvest keys for lateral movement to every host that trusts the corresponding public key.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: open/openat syscalls against private-key file paths, excluding the ssh-agent/ssh client itself.

detection_logic: Matches reads of files under ~/.ssh/ matching common private-key naming patterns, where the reading process is not ssh/ssh-agent/ssh-add and the reading user differs from the key owner.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=SYSCALL (syscall=open OR syscall=openat) key="ssh_key_access"
| rex field=_raw "exe=\"(?<exe>[^\"]+)\""
| where NOT match(exe, "(?i)/(ssh|ssh-agent|ssh-add)$")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| rex field=_raw "path=\"(?<target_path>[^\"]+/\.ssh/[^\"]+)\""
| table _time, host, auid, exe, target_path
tuning_guidance: Backup/imaging processes and configuration-management tooling that manages key deployment are the expected legitimate sources; exclude by binary.
investigation_steps: Identify the key file and its owning account.
Identify the reading process/auid.
If confirmed unauthorized, treat the private key as compromised and identify every host that trusts the corresponding public key.
response_guidance: Rotate the affected key pair everywhere it is trusted and investigate the reading account for compromise.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: IPA/Kerberos Keytab File Accessed Unexpectedly
description: Detects access to a Kerberos keytab file (/etc/krb5.keytab or a service-specific keytab) by a process other than the service it belongs to. A keytab is a long-lived, offline-usable credential; theft allows an attacker to impersonate the service principal indefinitely (or until the keytab is rotated) without needing an interactive Kerberos exchange.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: open/openat syscalls against keytab file paths.

detection_logic: Matches reads of *.keytab paths, excluding the expected owning service process.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=SYSCALL (syscall=open OR syscall=openat) key="keytab_access"
| rex field=_raw "exe=\"(?<exe>[^\"]+)\""
| rex field=_raw "path=\"(?<target_path>[^\"]+\.keytab)\""
| lookup keytab_owner_process.csv target_path OUTPUT expected_exe
| where exe!=expected_exe
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, exe, target_path
tuning_guidance: Maintenance/backup tooling and IPA client re-enrollment legitimately touch keytabs; maintain the expected-owner lookup and update it whenever a new service is provisioned.
investigation_steps: Identify the keytab and the principal it authenticates as.
Identify the reading process/auid.
Check IPA/KDC logs for subsequent authentication using the associated principal from an unexpected host.
response_guidance: Rotate the keytab (`ipa-getkeytab` re-issuance) immediately if access is unauthorized, and audit all authentication using the associated principal since the access.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Suspicious LD_PRELOAD Environment Variable or /etc/ld.so.preload Entry
description: Detects a write to /etc/ld.so.preload (system-wide, affects every dynamically-linked process) or an unusual LD_PRELOAD environment variable set on a privileged process. This is the classic Linux userspace-rootkit technique: a malicious shared library is loaded before all others and can hook libc functions (e.g. readdir, to hide files/processes from ls and ps) transparently to every process on the system.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: Writes to /etc/ld.so.preload; process environment capture for LD_PRELOAD (requires auditd's -e/--environment support or EXECVE environment logging where configured).

detection_logic: Watches writes to /etc/ld.so.preload directly (the highest-confidence signal, since this file should essentially always be empty on a RHEL host) and flags any non-empty content.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=PATH path="/etc/ld.so.preload"
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, path
tuning_guidance: No known legitimate enterprise use case touches this file in steady state; treat any write as page-now.
investigation_steps: Read the file's new content to identify the referenced shared library.
Locate and analyze the referenced .so file.
Identify auid.
response_guidance: Treat as a confirmed rootkit indicator: isolate the host, do not trust ps/ls output from it, and rebuild from known-good media after forensic collection.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1574.006: Dynamic Linker Hijacking

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Process Executed From a Deleted (Memory-Only) Binary
description: Detects a running process whose executable path resolves to '(deleted)' - meaning the binary on disk was removed after the process started, leaving only the in-memory copy. This is a well-known anti-forensics technique (also achievable directly via memfd_create) that prevents responders from recovering the executable from disk for analysis.

data_sources.name: Process inventory scan / auditd
data_sources.description: Requires a periodic process scan (comparing /proc/*/exe against the on-disk path) fed into Splunk, since this state is not directly logged by auditd.

detection_logic: A scheduled scan enumerates /proc/*/exe for every running process and flags any where the symlink target is suffixed ' (deleted)'.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=process_scan:deleted_exe
| table _time, host, pid, exe_path, comm
tuning_guidance: Legitimate software upgrades in place (a running daemon whose package was upgraded without a restart) produce this state harmlessly and are the dominant false-positive source; correlate against recent package-update activity for the exact binary before escalating.
investigation_steps: Attempt to dump the process memory for the deleted binary (`gdb`/`cat /proc/<pid>/exe > recovered_binary` while the process is still running) before it terminates.
Identify the parent process and command line.
Check whether a package update legitimately explains the state.
response_guidance: If not explained by a pending service restart after a package upgrade, treat as a rootkit/implant indicator and begin incident response.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: memfd_create Used for In-Memory Execution
description: Detects use of the memfd_create syscall to create an anonymous, memory-backed file descriptor and then execute it (the 'fileless' Linux execution technique popularized by tools like execve-via-memfd loaders). Because the executed code never touches disk, traditional file-based scanning and fapolicyd's path-based trust model cannot see it.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: memfd_create syscall, ideally correlated with a subsequent execveat targeting the resulting fd (/proc/self/fd/N).

detection_logic: Matches the memfd_create syscall directly; a stronger implementation correlates it with a subsequent execveat call referencing a memfd path within the same process.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=SYSCALL syscall=memfd_create
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| rex field=_raw "exe=\"(?<exe>[^\"]+)\""
| lookup approved_memfd_users.csv exe OUTPUT is_approved
| where isnull(is_approved)
| table _time, host, auid, exe
tuning_guidance: A small number of legitimate runtimes (some container tooling, some JIT-heavy language runtimes, systemd itself in some paths) use memfd_create; maintain an allowlist and expect to tune meaningfully at rollout.
investigation_steps: Identify the calling process and its full ancestry.
Check for a subsequent execveat call on the same process.
Attempt live memory analysis if the process is still running.
response_guidance: Treat as a high-confidence fileless-execution indicator once tuned; isolate and investigate the host.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1620: Reflective Code Loading

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Process Name Masquerading as a System Process
description: Detects a process whose command name (comm) matches a well-known system process (e.g. [kworker/0:1], systemd, sshd) but whose executable path does not match the expected system binary location - a masquerading technique to blend into `ps` output reviewed by an administrator or automated monitoring.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: EXECVE records showing comm/exe mismatch against expected system paths.

detection_logic: Joins process comm against a lookup of expected exe paths for well-known system process names, flagging any mismatch.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "comm=\"(?<comm>[^\"]+)\""
| rex field=_raw "exe=\"(?<exe>[^\"]+)\""
| lookup expected_process_paths.csv comm OUTPUT expected_exe
| where isnotnull(expected_exe) AND exe!=expected_exe
| table _time, host, comm, exe
tuning_guidance: Kernel worker thread names ([kworker/N:M]) are dynamically numbered and should be excluded from strict path matching (they have no exe path); focus this rule on named daemons like sshd, systemd, crond.
investigation_steps: Identify the actual executable and its origin.
Check the process's parent and children for further context.
Compare the binary's hash against the legitimate system binary.
response_guidance: Treat as a high-confidence masquerading indicator; isolate the host and investigate.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Cryptomining Process or Known Mining Pool Connection
description: Detects execution of a known cryptomining binary (xmrig and common aliases) or a network connection to a known mining-pool port/protocol pattern (stratum+tcp://). Resource hijacking for cryptomining is one of the most common monetization paths for opportunistic Linux compromises, since it requires no further post-exploitation effort beyond initial access.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: EXECVE records for known miner binary names/arguments.

detection_logic: Matches EXECVE command lines against known miner binary names and the stratum protocol URI pattern used by virtually all mining-pool clients.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "a0=\"(?<argv0>[^\"]+)\""
| where match(argv0, "(?i)(xmrig|minerd|cpuminer|ccminer)") OR match(_raw, "stratum\+tcp://")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, _raw
tuning_guidance: No legitimate enterprise use case; this should be a near-zero false-positive, page-now detection.
investigation_steps: Identify how the miner was delivered (correlate with RHEL-055/RHEL-056 for the delivery mechanism).
Identify the wallet address / pool from the command line for threat-intel correlation.
Check for persistence mechanisms installed alongside the miner (cron, systemd service).
response_guidance: Kill the process, remove associated persistence, and treat as confirmed compromise - investigate for a broader foothold beyond the opportunistic miner.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Mass File Deletion in a Short Window
description: Detects an unusually high rate of file-deletion syscalls from a single process/session in a short window, consistent with `rm -rf` against a large directory tree, a wiper, or early-stage ransomware clearing recovery points before encryption.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: unlink/unlinkat syscall volume per process/session.

detection_logic: Counts unlink/unlinkat syscall events per process/session in a rolling window and flags bursts well above normal interactive/administrative deletion rates.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=SYSCALL (syscall=unlink OR syscall=unlinkat)
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| rex field=_raw "exe=\"(?<exe>[^\"]+)\""
| bin _time span=1m
| stats count as deletions by _time, host, auid, exe
| where deletions >= 200
tuning_guidance: Build/cleanup jobs, log-rotation housekeeping scripts, and package uninstalls can legitimately delete many files quickly; exclude known cleanup automation by exe/auid and tune the threshold to the host's normal ceiling.
investigation_steps: Identify the process and what directory tree was targeted.
Identify auid.
Check whether this correlates with a broader destructive sequence (backup/snapshot deletion, service stops) per RH-X-010.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, isolate the host immediately - this pattern frequently precedes or accompanies ransomware/wiper impact - and assess backup integrity.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Disk-Wiping Utility Executed (shred, wipefs, dd to a block device)
description: Detects execution of shred, wipefs, or `dd` with a block device as the output target - tools whose entire purpose is irreversible data destruction. Legitimate use is limited to a narrow set of decommissioning/secure-erase procedures; any other occurrence is a critical impact indicator.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: EXECVE records for shred/wipefs/dd.

detection_logic: Matches EXECVE for shred and wipefs unconditionally, and dd specifically where the output file (of=) targets a block device path (/dev/sd*, /dev/nvme*, /dev/mapper/*, /dev/vd*).
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "a0=\"(?<argv0>[^\"]+)\""
| where argv0="shred" OR argv0="wipefs" OR (argv0="dd" AND match(_raw,"of=/dev/(sd|nvme|vd|mapper)"))
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, argv0, _raw
tuning_guidance: Decommissioning/secure-erase runbooks are the only expected source; require this to always correlate with a documented decommission ticket, and treat any occurrence outside that process as an emergency.
investigation_steps: Identify the target device/path and what data/filesystem it held.
Identify auid.
Check for a decommission ticket covering this exact host/device.
response_guidance: If no decommission ticket exists, treat as an active destructive attack: isolate the host immediately, halt any further disk activity if possible, and begin data-recovery/incident-response procedures.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: LVM Volume or Snapshot Removed
description: Detects use of `lvremove` to delete a logical volume or LVM snapshot. Attackers (and ransomware in particular) remove snapshots and backup volumes specifically to inhibit recovery before or after encrypting/destroying primary data.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: lvremove invocation via EXECVE.

detection_logic: Matches EXECVE records for lvremove.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=EXECVE
| rex field=_raw "a0=\"(?<argv0>[^\"]+)\""
| where argv0="lvremove"
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, _raw
tuning_guidance: Legitimate storage-management operations (freeing space, decommissioning a volume) do this routinely; correlate against a change ticket and pay particular attention to removal of anything with 'snap' or 'backup' in its name.
investigation_steps: Identify the removed volume/snapshot name and what it contained.
Identify auid.
Check whether this follows or precedes other destructive activity (RHEL-068, RHEL-069).
response_guidance: If unauthorized and a snapshot/backup volume, treat as a recovery-inhibition step within an active destructive attack and escalate immediately.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1490: Inhibit System Recovery

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Repeated Kerberos Pre-Authentication Failures
description: Detects a burst of Kerberos pre-authentication (AS-REQ) failures against the IPA KDC for a single principal or source, indicating password-guessing/brute-force activity against the identity backbone that every RHEL host, service, and application in the domain ultimately trusts.

data_sources.name: krb5kdc
data_sources.description: The KDC logs every AS-REQ/TGS-REQ with its result, including PREAUTH_FAILED for bad passwords.

detection_logic: Counts PREAUTH_FAILED events per principal/source in a rolling window against the KDC log.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:krb5kdc "PREAUTH_FAILED"
| rex field=_raw "for (?<principal>\S+@\S+),.*from (?<src_ip>[\d\.:]+)"
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count as failures by _time, src_ip, principal
| where failures >= 8
tuning_guidance: Expired-password lockout loops from misconfigured automation (a service that hasn't picked up a rotated password) are the primary false-positive source; identify and fix the offending automation rather than suppressing the alert.
investigation_steps: Identify src_ip and whether it is a known client host or an unexpected source.
Check for a subsequent successful AS-REQ for the same principal (IPA-002).
Check whether the same source is attacking multiple principals (password spray) vs. one principal repeatedly (targeted brute force).
response_guidance: Lock the targeted principal if failures continue, and block/investigate the source host.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Successful Kerberos Authentication Following Repeated Failures
description: Detects a successful Kerberos AS-REQ for a principal that recently produced multiple PREAUTH_FAILED events from the same source - the domain-identity equivalent of RHEL-002, and arguably higher-impact since a compromised IPA principal can authenticate to every service across the fleet that trusts the realm.

data_sources.name: krb5kdc
data_sources.description: Correlates PREAUTH_FAILED and successful AS-REQ (ISSUE) events for the same principal/source.

detection_logic: Joins a successful ISSUE (TGT issued) event to a preceding burst of PREAUTH_FAILED events for the same principal and source within a short window.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:krb5kdc "ISSUE"
| rex field=_raw "for (?<principal>\S+@\S+),.*from (?<src_ip>[\d\.:]+)"
| rename _time as success_time
| join type=inner principal, src_ip
    [ search index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:krb5kdc "PREAUTH_FAILED"
      | rex field=_raw "for (?<principal>\S+@\S+),.*from (?<src_ip>[\d\.:]+)"
      | bin _time span=15m
      | stats count as prior_failures by _time, principal, src_ip
      | where prior_failures >= 5 ]
| table success_time, principal, src_ip, prior_failures
tuning_guidance: Users mistyping a password before it locks in a cached credential manager can trigger this at low volume; tune the failure threshold per your typical user error rate.
investigation_steps: Confirm with the principal's owner whether the authentication was expected.
Immediately review what the principal accessed after obtaining its TGT (service-ticket requests).
Check for privilege-relevant group membership on the compromised principal (admins group).
response_guidance: Treat as a likely-compromised identity: reset the principal's Kerberos password/keytab, review all service tickets issued under it since compromise, and force re-authentication fleet-wide if the principal holds privileged access.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: IPA Administrator Login
description: Detects authentication to the IPA web UI, API, or CLI (kinit) as a principal in the `admins` group. Because IPA administrators can create/modify any user, HBAC rule, sudo rule, or certificate in the domain, their authentication events warrant close, continuous review regardless of source.

data_sources.name: IPA httpd (web UI/API)
data_sources.description: IPA framework logs authenticated API calls with the acting principal.

data_sources.name: krb5kdc
data_sources.description: AS-REQ success events for admin-group principals.

detection_logic: Joins successful authentication events against a lookup of principals currently in the admins group.
spl:
index=ipa (sourcetype=ipa:krb5kdc "ISSUE") OR (sourcetype=ipa:httpd "200")
| rex field=_raw "(?<principal>\S+@\S+)"
| lookup ipa_admins_group.csv principal OUTPUT is_admin
| where is_admin=1
| rex field=_raw "from (?<src_ip>[\d\.:]+)"
| table _time, principal, src_ip
tuning_guidance: Expected daily admin activity will produce routine noise; the value is in the audit trail and in flagging deviations (unusual hour, unusual source) rather than suppressing entirely - pair with IPA-004 for the anomaly layer.
investigation_steps: Confirm src_ip against the admin's known workstation/jump host.
Review the actions performed during the session (subsequent IPA API calls).
Cross-reference against a change ticket if the session performed configuration changes.
response_guidance: No routine response needed for expected admin activity; escalate immediately if source or timing is anomalous.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: IPA Administrator Login From Unusual Source Host
description: Detects an admins-group principal authenticating from a source IP not in its established baseline. Combines the high-value target (an IPA administrator) with the first-seen-source anomaly technique for a high-priority alert.

data_sources.name: krb5kdc / IPA httpd
data_sources.description: Source IP of authentication events for admin principals.

detection_logic: Baseline implementation: compares the source IP of an admin-group authentication against a maintained per-principal lookup of known-good sources.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:krb5kdc "ISSUE"
| rex field=_raw "(?<principal>\S+@\S+).*from (?<src_ip>[\d\.:]+)"
| lookup ipa_admins_group.csv principal OUTPUT is_admin
| where is_admin=1
| lookup admin_src_baseline.csv principal, src_ip OUTPUT is_known
| where isnull(is_known)
| table _time, principal, src_ip
tuning_guidance: New jump-host rollouts and admin travel are the main legitimate sources; keep the baseline lookup current and expect this to be lower-noise than the equivalent RHEL detection since there are far fewer admin principals than total users.
investigation_steps: Verify with the admin directly whether this was expected.
Review actions taken during the session immediately.
Check for other RH-X correlation signals (subsequent privileged automation execution).
response_guidance: Treat as urgent; if unconfirmed, disable the principal pending verification and review all recent changes made under it.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Authentication for a Disabled IPA User
description: Detects a successful (or even attempted) Kerberos authentication for a principal marked disabled/locked in IPA. A successful authentication here would indicate a serious IPA-level inconsistency or tampering (e.g. a replica out of sync, or a lockout bypass); an attempted authentication indicates someone still trying to use a credential that should no longer work (e.g. a recently-offboarded employee, or an attacker who doesn't know the account was disabled).

data_sources.name: krb5kdc + IPA user status
data_sources.description: Authentication events joined against current IPA account status.

detection_logic: Joins authentication events (success or failure) against a lookup of currently-disabled principals, refreshed frequently from `ipa user-find --disabled`.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:krb5kdc ("ISSUE" OR "PREAUTH_FAILED" OR "CLIENT_NOT_FOUND")
| rex field=_raw "(?<principal>\S+@\S+)"
| lookup ipa_disabled_users.csv principal OUTPUT is_disabled
| where is_disabled=1
| table _time, principal, _raw
tuning_guidance: A short propagation delay between disabling an account and replication to all KDC replicas can produce a handful of benign near-miss events; expect this to clear within the normal IPA replication interval.
investigation_steps: Confirm the account's disabled status is correctly replicated across all IPA replicas.
If a success was logged, treat as a P1 - investigate immediately how a disabled account authenticated.
Check for a corresponding recent enable/disable toggle that might explain a race condition.
response_guidance: Escalate any successful authentication for a disabled account immediately; for failed attempts, monitor for a pattern suggesting the credential is still being actively used by a former employee or attacker.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: IPA User Account Created
description: Detects creation of a new IPA user account via `ipa user-add`, the web UI, or the API. Establishes a baseline audit trail for every identity created in the domain; attackers with sufficient IPA privilege create accounts as a durable, centrally-trusted persistence mechanism that grants access across the entire managed fleet at once.

data_sources.name: IPA API/httpd audit
data_sources.description: Every IPA framework write operation is logged with the acting principal, the operation (user_add), and the target.

detection_logic: Filters IPA framework audit records for the user_add operation.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:httpd "user_add"
| rex field=_raw "principal=(?<actor_principal>\S+)"
| rex field=_raw "uid=(?<target_user>\S+)"
| table _time, actor_principal, target_user
tuning_guidance: Correlate with Satellite/AAP-driven provisioning workflows and HR onboarding processes to distinguish expected new-hire provisioning from unexpected creation.
investigation_steps: Identify actor_principal and confirm they hold legitimate user-provisioning rights.
Review the new account's initial group memberships and any sudo/HBAC rules that apply to it.
Check whether the account was created outside business hours or from an unusual admin session.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, disable the account immediately and investigate the actor principal.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: admins Group Membership Changed
description: Detects a principal being added to (or removed from) the `admins` group - IPA's highest-privilege group, whose members can modify any object in the domain including HBAC rules, sudo rules, certificates, and other users. This is functionally the IPA equivalent of RHEL wheel-group manipulation, but with domain-wide rather than single-host scope.

data_sources.name: IPA API/httpd audit
data_sources.description: group_add_member/group_remove_member operations targeting the admins group.

detection_logic: Filters IPA framework audit records for group membership operations where the target group is admins.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:httpd ("group_add_member" OR "group_remove_member") "cn=admins"
| rex field=_raw "principal=(?<actor_principal>\S+)"
| rex field=_raw "member_user=(?<target_user>\S+)"
| table _time, actor_principal, target_user, _raw
tuning_guidance: This should be one of the lowest-volume, highest-scrutiny events in the entire environment; every occurrence should be tied to a documented, approved access request with no exceptions.
investigation_steps: Identify actor_principal and confirm formal approval exists for the change.
Review the target account's recent authentication history for any compromise indicators.
Check what the newly-admin account does immediately after gaining membership.
response_guidance: Revert unauthorized membership immediately; treat both the actor and target accounts as potentially compromised pending investigation.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: IPA User Password Reset by an Administrator
description: Detects an administrator resetting another user's password. Legitimate for help-desk password-reset workflows, but also how an attacker with IPA admin access takes over a target account without needing to know its original password - especially concerning for high-privilege target accounts.

data_sources.name: IPA API/httpd audit
data_sources.description: passwd operation logged with acting principal and target user.

detection_logic: Filters IPA framework audit records for password-reset operations where actor != target.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:httpd "passwd"
| rex field=_raw "principal=(?<actor_principal>\S+)"
| rex field=_raw "uid=(?<target_user>\S+)"
| where actor_principal!=target_user
| table _time, actor_principal, target_user
tuning_guidance: Help-desk staff performing routine resets are the expected volume; escalate specifically when the target account is privileged (admins group, service account) since that combination is much less commonly legitimate.
investigation_steps: Confirm a help-desk ticket exists for the reset.
Check whether the target account is privileged.
Check whether the target account authenticated with the new password shortly after (confirming takeover) from an unexpected source.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, re-reset the password through a verified channel and notify the legitimate account owner.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: New or Overly Broad HBAC Rule Created
description: Detects creation of a Host-Based Access Control (HBAC) rule, with elevated severity when the rule uses a wildcard/all-hosts or all-services scope. HBAC rules are IPA's centralized authorization layer for which users can access which hosts via which services (typically sshd); an overly broad rule can grant domain-wide access with a single change.

data_sources.name: IPA API/httpd audit
data_sources.description: hbacrule_add and related operations.

detection_logic: Filters HBAC rule-creation events and flags those whose hostcategory or servicecategory is set to 'all'.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:httpd "hbacrule_add"
| rex field=_raw "principal=(?<actor_principal>\S+)"
| rex field=_raw "cn=(?<rule_name>[^,]+)"
| eval broad=if(match(_raw,"hostcategory=all") OR match(_raw,"servicecategory=all"),1,0)
| table _time, actor_principal, rule_name, broad
tuning_guidance: Legitimate break-glass or fleet-wide maintenance-access rules occasionally use broad scope by design; require these to be explicitly time-boxed/disabled outside maintenance windows rather than left permanently enabled.
investigation_steps: Review the rule's user/host/service scope in full.
Identify actor_principal and confirm approval.
Check whether the rule is enabled and check for authentication events that immediately relied on it.
response_guidance: Disable or narrow the rule if unauthorized, and audit any access already granted under it.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: HBAC Rule Modified to Add Privileged Access
description: Detects an existing HBAC rule being modified to add a new user/group or host/hostgroup to its scope, which can silently expand who can reach which systems without the more visible signal of creating an entirely new rule.

data_sources.name: IPA API/httpd audit
data_sources.description: hbacrule_add_user, hbacrule_add_host, hbacrule_add_service operations.

detection_logic: Filters HBAC rule-member-addition operations.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:httpd ("hbacrule_add_user" OR "hbacrule_add_host" OR "hbacrule_add_service")
| rex field=_raw "principal=(?<actor_principal>\S+)"
| rex field=_raw "cn=(?<rule_name>[^,]+)"
| table _time, actor_principal, rule_name, _raw
tuning_guidance: Routine access-request fulfillment is the expected source; correlate against a ticketing system reference if your IPA deployment captures change reasons.
investigation_steps: Identify exactly what was added to the rule's scope.
Confirm approval for the specific access granted.
Check whether the newly-granted access was used immediately.
response_guidance: Revert unauthorized additions and review recent access under the rule.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: New IPA Sudo Rule Created
description: Detects creation of a centrally-managed IPA sudo rule, which SSSD propagates to every RHEL client in scope. A single malicious or overly broad sudo rule can grant root-equivalent access on many hosts simultaneously - the identity-plane equivalent of an AAP or Satellite fleet-wide push.

data_sources.name: IPA API/httpd audit
data_sources.description: sudorule_add operation.

detection_logic: Filters IPA framework audit records for sudorule_add.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:httpd "sudorule_add"
| rex field=_raw "principal=(?<actor_principal>\S+)"
| rex field=_raw "cn=(?<rule_name>[^,]+)"
| table _time, actor_principal, rule_name
tuning_guidance: Legitimate operational sudo rules are created regularly by platform teams; the real value is in the follow-on detections (IPA-012, IPA-013) that flag dangerously broad scope.
investigation_steps: Review the rule's command, host, and user scope once populated.
Identify actor_principal.
Cross-reference with a change ticket.
response_guidance: No immediate action for a narrowly-scoped, approved rule; escalate per IPA-012/IPA-013 for broad rules.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: IPA Sudo Rule Grants All-Host Scope
description: Detects an IPA sudo rule whose host category is set to 'all', meaning the rule applies to every host managed by SSSD/IPA in the domain. Combined with a permissive command set, this is one of the single most impactful configuration changes possible in a Red Hat identity-managed fleet.

data_sources.name: IPA API/httpd audit
data_sources.description: sudorule_add/sudorule_mod operations with hostcategory=all.

detection_logic: Filters sudo-rule create/modify operations where hostcategory is set to all.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:httpd ("sudorule_add" OR "sudorule_mod") "hostcategory=all"
| rex field=_raw "principal=(?<actor_principal>\S+)"
| rex field=_raw "cn=(?<rule_name>[^,]+)"
| table _time, actor_principal, rule_name
tuning_guidance: A small number of legitimate break-glass sudo rules are intentionally fleet-wide; these should be NOPASSWD-restricted to a specific emergency command and disabled outside active use, not standing.
investigation_steps: Review the exact command(s) and users the rule grants.
Confirm executive/security approval for fleet-wide sudo scope.
Check for sudo executions across the fleet under this rule (RH-X-002 pattern) immediately after creation.
response_guidance: Narrow the rule's host scope immediately unless it is an approved, documented break-glass mechanism; treat unapproved fleet-wide sudo grants as a critical incident.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: IPA Sudo Rule Grants NOPASSWD All-Command Access
description: Detects an IPA sudo rule whose command category is 'all' combined with a NOPASSWD (no re-authentication required) run-as option - effectively unrestricted, password-less root access for every user/host in the rule's scope. This is the single most dangerous sudo-rule configuration IPA can express.

data_sources.name: IPA API/httpd audit
data_sources.description: sudorule_add/sudorule_mod operations with cmdcategory=all and a NOPASSWD sudo option.

detection_logic: Filters sudo-rule operations matching both cmdcategory=all and a !authenticate/NOPASSWD sudo option.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:httpd ("sudorule_add" OR "sudorule_mod") "cmdcategory=all" ("!authenticate" OR "NOPASSWD")
| rex field=_raw "principal=(?<actor_principal>\S+)"
| rex field=_raw "cn=(?<rule_name>[^,]+)"
| table _time, actor_principal, rule_name
tuning_guidance: Essentially never appropriate as a standing rule outside a narrowly-scoped, time-boxed break-glass mechanism; treat as an immediate hardening finding wherever discovered, not just on creation.
investigation_steps: Identify the exact users/hosts in scope.
Confirm any approval for this configuration.
Check for immediate sudo usage under the rule.
response_guidance: Remove the NOPASSWD/all-command combination immediately unless formally approved as break-glass, and require re-authentication for privileged sudo going forward.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Unusual Volume of TGT Requests From a Single Source
description: Detects a single source host requesting an unusually high number of distinct TGTs (for different principals) in a short window, which can indicate credential-stuffing against the KDC or an account-enumeration sweep using Kerberos as an oracle for valid usernames.

data_sources.name: krb5kdc
data_sources.description: AS-REQ volume and distinct-principal count per source.

detection_logic: Counts distinct principals requested from a single source IP in a rolling window.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:krb5kdc "AS-REQ"
| rex field=_raw "(?<principal>\S+@\S+).*from (?<src_ip>[\d\.:]+)"
| bin _time span=10m
| stats dc(principal) as distinct_principals by _time, src_ip
| where distinct_principals >= 15
tuning_guidance: A busy jump host or automation server legitimately authenticating as many different service accounts can trigger this; allowlist known multi-principal automation sources.
investigation_steps: Identify src_ip.
Review the specific principals targeted for a pattern (alphabetical sweep, common username list).
Check for any resulting successful authentications.
response_guidance: Investigate the source host; block if confirmed malicious and review for any successful compromises from the sweep.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Kerberos Credential Cache (ccache) File Accessed by an Unexpected Process
description: Detects a process other than the session's own Kerberos-aware tooling reading a user's credential cache file (typically /tmp/krb5cc_<uid> or KEYRING/KCM-backed). Theft of a live ccache lets an attacker impersonate the user's already-authenticated Kerberos session without needing the password at all, for as long as the tickets remain valid.

data_sources.name: auditd (on the RHEL client)
data_sources.description: open/openat syscalls against krb5cc_* paths.

detection_logic: Matches reads of krb5cc_* files where the reading process is not a standard Kerberos client tool and the reading UID differs from the ccache's owning UID.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=SYSCALL (syscall=open OR syscall=openat) key="ccache_access"
| rex field=_raw "exe=\"(?<exe>[^\"]+)\""
| where NOT match(exe, "(?i)/(kinit|klist|kdestroy|sssd|krb5)")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| rex field=_raw "path=\"(?<target_path>[^\"]*krb5cc_[^\"]*)\""
| table _time, host, auid, exe, target_path
tuning_guidance: Backup/monitoring agents reading /tmp indiscriminately are the main source; exclude by binary explicitly.
investigation_steps: Identify the reading process and auid.
If theft is confirmed, identify every service the stolen tickets could access before they expire.
Check for use of the stolen tickets from an unexpected source host.
response_guidance: Destroy the affected session's tickets (`kdestroy`), force re-authentication, and, if the ccache belonged to a privileged principal, treat as a domain-relevant compromise.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Keytab File Created or Replaced
description: Detects a new keytab being generated for a principal via `ipa-getkeytab`, or an existing keytab being replaced. Keytabs are long-lived, offline-usable credentials; an attacker who can request one for a privileged service principal gains durable access without ever needing to authenticate interactively.

data_sources.name: IPA API/httpd audit
data_sources.description: Keytab retrieval is logged as an IPA API operation tied to the requesting principal and target service.

detection_logic: Filters IPA framework audit records for keytab-retrieval operations.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:httpd "ipa-getkeytab"
| rex field=_raw "principal=(?<actor_principal>\S+)"
| rex field=_raw "target=(?<target_principal>\S+)"
| table _time, actor_principal, target_principal
tuning_guidance: Legitimate service provisioning (new host joining the domain, application service account setup) requests keytabs routinely; correlate against Satellite/AAP-driven host provisioning workflows.
investigation_steps: Identify actor_principal and target_principal.
Confirm the request corresponds to a documented provisioning event.
Check where the resulting keytab file was written and whether that host is expected to run the target service.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, re-issue (rotate) the keytab for the target principal immediately, invalidating the stolen copy.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: krb5.conf Modified on the KDC or a Client
description: Detects modification of /etc/krb5.conf. On a client, this can redirect a host to an attacker-controlled rogue KDC for the realm (enabling credential interception); on the KDC itself, it can weaken encryption-type requirements or ticket lifetime policy.

data_sources.name: auditd
data_sources.description: Write watch on /etc/krb5.conf and /etc/krb5.conf.d/.

detection_logic: Watches writes to the Kerberos client/server configuration path.
spl:
index=linux sourcetype=linux_audit type=PATH (path="/etc/krb5.conf" OR path="/etc/krb5.conf.d/*")
| rex field=_raw "auid=(?<auid>\d+)"
| table _time, host, auid, path
tuning_guidance: IPA client enrollment and configuration-management-driven Kerberos hardening legitimately manage this file; correlate against ipa-client-install runs and AAP job execution.
investigation_steps: Diff the file, paying particular attention to the kdc= and admin_server= realm mapping entries.
Identify auid.
If the KDC address changed, verify it still points at a legitimate IPA server.
response_guidance: Revert unauthorized changes immediately; if a rogue KDC was configured, treat any authentication performed while it was active as potentially compromised.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1556: Modify Authentication Process

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Certificate Issued for a Privileged Service Principal
description: Detects the IPA-integrated Dogtag Certificate Authority issuing a new certificate for a host or service principal, with elevated attention on certificates issued for the KDC, LDAP, or CA's own service principals. A rogue certificate for a trusted service principal is a powerful impersonation/persistence primitive against every client that trusts the realm's CA.

data_sources.name: Dogtag CA audit log
data_sources.description: Dogtag emits a signed audit record for every certificate-issuance event including the requester and subject.

detection_logic: Filters CA audit records for CERT_REQUEST_PROCESSED events, flagging subjects matching high-value service principals.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=dogtag:ca_audit "CERT_REQUEST_PROCESSED"
| rex field=_raw "requestor=(?<actor_principal>\S+)"
| rex field=_raw "subject=\"(?<cert_subject>[^\"]+)\""
| lookup high_value_cert_principals.csv cert_subject OUTPUT is_high_value
| where is_high_value=1
| table _time, actor_principal, cert_subject
tuning_guidance: Certificate renewal (certmonger-driven auto-renewal) happens on a predictable schedule shortly before expiry; correlate issuance timing against the expected renewal window for the target principal.
investigation_steps: Confirm actor_principal held legitimate authority to request the certificate.
Verify the issuance falls within the expected renewal window rather than mid-lifetime.
Check where the resulting certificate/private key was deployed.
response_guidance: Revoke the certificate immediately if unauthorized (IPA-019) and re-issue through the proper process.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1649: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Certificate Revoked by CA Administrator
description: Detects a certificate being revoked. Legitimate for decommissioning or responding to a compromised key, but mass or unexpected revocation can also be used by an attacker to disrupt service authentication as a denial-of-service/impact action against the domain.

data_sources.name: Dogtag CA audit log
data_sources.description: CERT_STATUS_CHANGE_REQUEST_PROCESSED events for revocation.

detection_logic: Filters CA audit records for revocation events.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=dogtag:ca_audit "CERT_STATUS_CHANGE_REQUEST_PROCESSED" "revoked"
| rex field=_raw "requestor=(?<actor_principal>\S+)"
| rex field=_raw "subject=\"(?<cert_subject>[^\"]+)\""
| table _time, actor_principal, cert_subject
tuning_guidance: Routine host decommissioning generates expected revocations; escalate specifically on unusual volume (mass revocation) or revocation of an actively-used service certificate.
investigation_steps: Identify actor_principal and the revocation reason given.
Check whether the affected service/host is still in active production use.
If mass revocation, treat as a potential impact/DoS event.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, re-issue the certificate immediately to restore service; investigate the actor for compromise if the pattern suggests malicious intent.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1531: Account Access Removal

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Mass Certificate Revocation
description: Detects a burst of certificate revocations in a short window, which - unlike a single decommissioning revocation - is a strong indicator of a deliberate attack against domain-wide service authentication availability, since every service relying on a revoked certificate will fail TLS/mutual-auth handshakes until re-issued.

data_sources.name: Dogtag CA audit log
data_sources.description: Aggregate count of revocation events.

detection_logic: Counts distinct certificate revocations by actor in a rolling window.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=dogtag:ca_audit "CERT_STATUS_CHANGE_REQUEST_PROCESSED" "revoked"
| rex field=_raw "requestor=(?<actor_principal>\S+)"
| bin _time span=10m
| stats dc(_raw) as revocation_count by _time, actor_principal
| where revocation_count >= 5
tuning_guidance: A planned CA rollover or bulk decommissioning project is the only expected legitimate source and should be scheduled/communicated in advance.
investigation_steps: Identify actor_principal and whether a change window covers this activity.
Identify the scope of affected services and their business impact.
Correlate with any other CA administration activity from the same session.
response_guidance: Treat as an active incident: engage IR, re-issue critical service certificates on a priority basis, and investigate the actor account.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1531: Account Access Removal

author: Threat Detection Library

title: CA Configuration or Profile Modified
description: Detects a change to a Dogtag certificate profile (which controls what a given certificate request is permitted to contain - key usage, validity period, subject constraints) or core CA configuration. A weakened profile (e.g. permitting a longer validity period or removing subject constraints) can enable subsequent issuance of an overly-powerful rogue certificate.

data_sources.name: Dogtag CA / IPA audit
data_sources.description: Certificate profile modification operations.

detection_logic: Filters for profile-modification and CA configuration-change audit records.
spl:
index=ipa (sourcetype=dogtag:ca_audit "CONFIG_CERT_PROFILE" ) OR (sourcetype=ipa:httpd "certprofile_mod")
| rex field=_raw "requestor=(?<actor_principal>\S+)"
| rex field=_raw "profileId=(?<profile_id>\S+)"
| table _time, actor_principal, profile_id, _raw
tuning_guidance: Extremely rare in steady state outside of a deliberate, planned PKI change project; treat with the same scrutiny as any core trust-infrastructure modification.
investigation_steps: Diff the profile configuration for weakened constraints.
Identify actor_principal.
Check for certificate issuance under the modified profile immediately after the change.
response_guidance: Revert to the known-good profile configuration and audit any certificates issued while the weakened profile was active.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1553: Subvert Trust Controls

author: Threat Detection Library

title: 389 Directory Server Privileged Bind
description: Detects an LDAP bind as the Directory Manager account or another privileged DN directly against 389-ds, bypassing the Kerberos-fronted IPA framework entirely. Direct privileged LDAP access is typically reserved for emergency/break-glass use since it bypasses IPA's normal audit-friendly API layer.

data_sources.name: 389 Directory Server access log
data_sources.description: Every LDAP bind is logged with the bind DN, result, and source IP.

detection_logic: Filters access-log BIND operations where the bind DN matches Directory Manager or another known privileged DN.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:dirsrv "BIND" "cn=Directory Manager"
| rex field=_raw "conn=\d+ op=\d+ BIND dn=\"(?<bind_dn>[^\"]+)\""
| rex field=_raw "from (?<src_ip>[\d\.:]+)"
| table _time, bind_dn, src_ip
tuning_guidance: Break-glass procedures and some backup/replication tooling legitimately use Directory Manager binds; maintain an allowlist of expected source hosts and require any other use to be a documented emergency.
investigation_steps: Confirm src_ip against the break-glass allowlist.
Review what LDAP operations were performed during the bound session.
Check whether an IPA API-layer administrative alternative should have been used instead.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, rotate the Directory Manager password immediately and audit all directory changes made during the session.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Directory Server Access Control Instruction (ACI) Modified
description: Detects a change to a directory ACI (389-ds's native access-control mechanism, layered beneath IPA's RBAC/permission abstractions). Direct ACI manipulation can grant read/write access to sensitive directory subtrees that IPA's higher-level permission model would not normally allow, and is far less commonly reviewed than IPA role/privilege assignments.

data_sources.name: 389 Directory Server access/audit log
data_sources.description: MOD operations targeting the aci attribute.

detection_logic: Filters MOD operations where the modified attribute is aci.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:dirsrv "MOD" "aci"
| rex field=_raw "conn=\d+ op=\d+ MOD dn=\"(?<target_dn>[^\"]+)\""
| table _time, target_dn, _raw
tuning_guidance: IPA's own framework manages most ACIs as a side effect of role/permission changes made through the normal API; a direct LDAP-level ACI modification bypassing that framework is inherently higher-suspicion.
investigation_steps: Identify the modifying bind DN and target subtree.
Review the ACI's new grant scope.
Check for subsequent access to the newly-exposed subtree.
response_guidance: Revert unauthorized ACI changes and investigate the modifying account.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Bulk LDAP Modification in a Short Window
description: Detects an unusually high volume of LDAP MOD/ADD/DELETE operations from a single bind in a short window, which can indicate a scripted attack (mass privilege grant, mass account manipulation) or a directory-wide destructive operation.

data_sources.name: 389 Directory Server access log
data_sources.description: Per-connection operation volume.

detection_logic: Counts write operations (MOD/ADD/DEL) per bind DN in a rolling window.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:dirsrv ("MOD" OR "ADD" OR "DEL")
| rex field=_raw "conn=(?<conn>\d+)"
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count as write_ops by _time, conn
| where write_ops >= 100
tuning_guidance: Bulk provisioning scripts (initial fleet onboarding, a large HR-driven batch of new hires) are the expected legitimate source; correlate against a documented bulk-operation change window.
investigation_steps: Identify the bind DN behind the connection.
Review a sample of the operations performed for pattern (mass group additions, mass deletions).
Check for any correlation with AAP/Satellite automation performing the bulk change.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, halt the source session/account immediately and assess the scope of directory changes made.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Unusual LDAP Search / Directory Enumeration
description: Detects a high-volume or unusually broad-scope LDAP search (e.g. a base-DN wildcard search returning most/all directory entries), consistent with an attacker enumerating the full user/group/host population to plan further attacks (identify privileged accounts, map group structure, discover service principals).

data_sources.name: 389 Directory Server access log
data_sources.description: SRCH operations with their base DN, filter, and result count.

detection_logic: Flags SRCH operations whose returned entry count exceeds a high threshold relative to normal application query patterns.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:dirsrv "SRCH"
| rex field=_raw "conn=(?<conn>\d+).*base=\"(?<base_dn>[^\"]+)\""
| rex field=_raw "nentries=(?<result_count>\d+)"
| where result_count >= 500
| table _time, conn, base_dn, result_count
tuning_guidance: SSSD's own periodic full-refresh queries and legitimate reporting/inventory tooling can produce large result sets; allowlist known SSSD/reporting service binds.
investigation_steps: Identify the bind DN behind the connection.
Check whether the source is a known application or an unfamiliar client.
Cross-reference with subsequent targeted activity against specific accounts identified in the enumeration.
response_guidance: Investigate the source; if a human/interactive session, question why bulk enumeration was needed and treat with elevated suspicion.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1069: Permission Groups Discovery

author: Threat Detection Library

title: IPA-Integrated DNS Record Created or Modified
description: Detects creation or modification of a DNS record (A/AAAA/CNAME/SRV) in IPA-integrated DNS, particularly changes to records for critical infrastructure names (the IPA servers themselves, wildcard entries, or well-known application hostnames) that could redirect clients to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

data_sources.name: IPA API/httpd audit
data_sources.description: dnsrecord_add/dnsrecord_mod operations.

detection_logic: Filters DNS record create/modify operations, with a lookup flagging changes to critical hostnames.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:httpd ("dnsrecord_add" OR "dnsrecord_mod")
| rex field=_raw "principal=(?<actor_principal>\S+)"
| rex field=_raw "idnsname=(?<record_name>\S+)"
| lookup critical_dns_names.csv record_name OUTPUT is_critical
| table _time, actor_principal, record_name, is_critical
tuning_guidance: Routine application deployment creates new DNS records regularly; the is_critical flag from the lookup is the primary severity driver - low-value hostnames are lower priority than changes to core infrastructure names.
investigation_steps: Identify what changed and whether it points at expected infrastructure.
Identify actor_principal.
For critical-name changes, verify with the infrastructure team before treating as benign.
response_guidance: Revert unauthorized DNS changes immediately, particularly for critical/wildcard records.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Wildcard DNS Record Created
description: Detects creation of a wildcard (*) DNS record in an IPA-managed zone, which causes every unmatched subdomain query to resolve to the specified target - a technique attackers use to intercept traffic for arbitrary, not-yet-registered internal hostnames.

data_sources.name: IPA API/httpd audit
data_sources.description: dnsrecord_add operation with a wildcard record name.

detection_logic: Filters DNS record-creation events where the record name is literally '*'.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:httpd "dnsrecord_add" "idnsname=\*"
| rex field=_raw "principal=(?<actor_principal>\S+)"
| rex field=_raw "zone=(?<zone>\S+)"
| table _time, actor_principal, zone
tuning_guidance: Rare, deliberate legitimate use exists for some internal wildcard-DNS test/dev environments; require explicit documented justification for any occurrence in a production zone.
investigation_steps: Identify the target the wildcard resolves to.
Identify actor_principal.
Check for anomalous DNS resolution complaints/traffic redirection reports from the affected zone.
response_guidance: Remove the wildcard record immediately unless explicitly approved, and investigate the actor.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Cross-Realm/AD Trust Created
description: Detects establishment of a new cross-realm Kerberos trust (most commonly to an Active Directory forest) via `ipa trust-add`. A trust relationship extends authentication reach across an entire foreign domain; an unauthorized trust can be used to bootstrap authentication paths from an attacker-controlled or already-compromised external domain directly into the Red Hat-managed environment.

data_sources.name: IPA API/httpd audit
data_sources.description: trust_add operation.

detection_logic: Filters IPA framework audit records for trust_add.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:httpd "trust_add"
| rex field=_raw "principal=(?<actor_principal>\S+)"
| rex field=_raw "cn=(?<trust_domain>[^,]+)"
| table _time, actor_principal, trust_domain
tuning_guidance: Trust establishment is a rare, deliberate architectural event that should always correspond to a planned integration project; there is essentially no scenario where this should occur unannounced.
investigation_steps: Confirm the trust was part of an approved integration project.
Identify actor_principal.
Review the trust's configured access scope (which AD groups/users gain access to which IPA resources).
response_guidance: If unauthorized, remove the trust immediately (`ipa trust-del`) and treat as a critical security incident.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Trust Configuration Modified (SID/Domain Mapping)
description: Detects a modification to an existing trust's configuration, particularly SID-to-IPA-group mapping (external group mapping) that determines which foreign-domain principals inherit which local privileges. A subtly modified mapping can grant an external, less-trusted identity IPA-side privileges without creating a whole new trust relationship.

data_sources.name: IPA API/httpd audit
data_sources.description: trust_mod and idrange-related operations.

detection_logic: Filters IPA framework audit records for trust_mod and associated ID-range modification operations.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:httpd ("trust_mod" OR "idrange_mod")
| rex field=_raw "principal=(?<actor_principal>\S+)"
| table _time, actor_principal, _raw
tuning_guidance: Legitimate periodic trust maintenance (renewing the trust password, adjusting UID ranges as the AD domain grows) occurs occasionally; correlate with a documented maintenance window.
investigation_steps: Diff the trust configuration for the specific mapping change.
Identify actor_principal.
Check for authentication from the newly-mapped foreign identities immediately after the change.
response_guidance: Revert unauthorized mapping changes immediately and audit access granted under the modified mapping.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: New IPA Replica Added
description: Detects a new replica being added to the IPA topology (`ipa-replica-install` / topology segment creation). A rogue replica receives a full copy of the directory (including password hashes and Kerberos key material for every principal) and, once established, is difficult to distinguish from a legitimate replica without careful topology review.

data_sources.name: IPA API/httpd audit
data_sources.description: topologysegment_add and related replica-registration operations.

detection_logic: Filters IPA framework audit records for topology segment / replica addition operations.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:httpd ("topologysegment_add" OR "server-conncheck")
| rex field=_raw "principal=(?<actor_principal>\S+)"
| table _time, actor_principal, _raw
tuning_guidance: Planned capacity/DR expansion is the only expected source and should always be a scheduled, communicated infrastructure change.
investigation_steps: Confirm the new replica host is an approved, hardened system under IT control.
Identify actor_principal.
Verify the replica's certificate and topology role are as expected.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, remove the replica from the topology immediately and treat as a critical incident - assume full directory contents (including password hashes) were exposed.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Replication Failure or Unexpected Replication Source
description: Detects a replication agreement reporting errors, or replication traffic arriving from a source not in the known topology, which can indicate topology tampering, a rogue replica attempt, or a legitimate but urgent operational issue (network partition, certificate expiry) that itself creates a window of directory inconsistency an attacker could exploit.

data_sources.name: 389 Directory Server error log
data_sources.description: Replication agreement status and errors.

detection_logic: Filters directory server error-log entries for replication failure messages and cross-references the reporting source against the known topology.
spl:
index=ipa sourcetype=ipa:dirsrv_errors "replication" ("error" OR "failed")
| lookup known_ipa_topology.csv host OUTPUT is_known_replica
| table _time, host, is_known_replica, _raw
tuning_guidance: Transient network issues cause brief replication errors regularly; escalate specifically on sustained failures (>15 minutes) or any traffic from a host not in the known topology at all.
investigation_steps: Identify the specific replica and error condition.
Confirm the source host against the documented topology.
Check for a broader pattern of topology tampering (IPA-030) around the same time.
response_guidance: Resolve the underlying replication issue; if the source is unrecognized, treat as a likely rogue-replica attempt and investigate immediately.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1082: System Information Discovery

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Repeated AAP Controller Login Failures
description: Detects a burst of failed login attempts against the Automation Controller UI or API for a single user or source. Because Controller sessions can launch privileged jobs across the entire managed fleet, its authentication surface deserves the same brute-force monitoring rigor as the identity plane itself.

data_sources.name: AAP activity stream / API access log
data_sources.description: Controller logs authentication attempts with outcome, username, and source IP.

detection_logic: Counts failed authentication events per user/source in a rolling window.
spl:
index=aap sourcetype=aap:api_access status=401 path="/api/*/login*"
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count as failures by _time, user, src_ip
| where failures >= 8
tuning_guidance: A CI pipeline using a stale API token will retry and fail repeatedly; identify and fix the offending pipeline rather than suppressing the alert broadly.
investigation_steps: Identify src_ip and whether it is a known automation caller.
Check for a subsequent successful login for the same user (AAP-002).
Check whether multiple users are being targeted from the same source (spray pattern).
response_guidance: Lock the account after continued failures and investigate/block the source.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Successful AAP Login Following Repeated Failures
description: Detects a successful Controller authentication for a user/source pair that recently produced multiple failures - a compromised-credential indicator on the platform that can, in the worst case, be used to push commands to every RHEL host in inventory.

data_sources.name: AAP activity stream / API access log
data_sources.description: Correlates 401 and 200 login responses for the same user/source.

detection_logic: Joins a successful login to a preceding burst of failures for the same user/source within a short window.
spl:
index=aap sourcetype=aap:api_access status=200 path="/api/*/login*"
| rename _time as success_time
| join type=inner user, src_ip
